This is a goldmine. Key facts confirmed:

**Ultimate (Pi Durable) persistence:**
- Everything (conversation, tool calls, subagents, documents) committed to SQLite before shown (`state.sqlite` per project home, plus `trace.sqlite`).
- The host is a long-running process; the web UI connects over HTTP. Restart = core swap (`self` extension's `restart` tool is replay-safe; supervisor `pnpm start` prepares a new generation, type-checked, then swaps; busy agents resume in the new process).
- Crash resume: a run resumes from its last checkpoint; replay-safe tools rerun; others report "interrupted". Durable tasks (effects) run at-least-once with idempotency keys.
- Chapters (dream): rotate the SQLite database ("the-beginning" → new chapter), carrying a seed (memories, learned lines, handover, open to-dos, questions, automations) into a fresh DB. Like human memory consolidation.
- Cache management is a first-class, engineered concern: the pi-claude-code patch rebuilds replay cache markers within Claude's four-block limit; inline-tools beta to avoid the merged-system-prompt fallback that "put every section or tool change at the start of the cached prefix, so each landing rewrote @ultimate's whole cache (17 rewrites, 5.8M tokens in one day)". Prompt sections deliberately never change ("its text never changes, because every system prompt change costs the prompt cache"). keep-warm pings to renew the 1h cache. recall injects memories "at the same position... which keeps the cached prompt prefix. The system prompt never changes."
- Memories: lineage.memory (≤150, decisions/facts/lessons, slugs), brief injected into new branches, memory tool with query via classify (TypeSafe), memory review branches, dream pruning. Recall re-injects into @ultimate mid-conversation.
- Catch-up on resume: "Meanwhile in #R's tree" note before an input after idle.

**DSH resume:**
- Sessions are event-sourced append-only logs; persisted via dsh-session-persistence-jsonl (JSONL + zstd, leases for single-writer, format migrations v0→v4). SQLite only as a query index (dsh-session-query-sqlite) and JSON storage domains for projection cache.
- Resume: agent registry `resume()` → `persistence.open(id,'write')` (write lease excludes concurrent resume) → cold read of the full log → interruptedTurnClosers() synthetically closes a crashed turn (missing tool errors, step/end, turn/end) → Session seeded with the full log → agent initialized source 'resume' → first request logs request/header reason 'resume'.
- Projection cache: durable per-session checkpoints so a cold read folds projections from a checkpoint instead of replaying everything; rows can be stale (seq watermark) but never wrong; ver mismatch discards.
- Durability: session-checkpoint-policy delays adapter dispatch until the request prefix is durable (flush before first chunk). So the "commit-before-show" discipline exists in DSH too, in the request direction.
- Compaction: compaction-basic default thresholdRatio 0.8, retainRatio 0.16; automatic on pressure or provider-confirmed overflow; manual via /compact; replaces surface span with one summary node; compaction and tool-result pruning rewrite the prefix → prefix-binding digests for Anthropic signed thinking (stale thinking dropped when digest mismatches).
- Request series: `startsSeries` marks a new series when surface changed since last request / tools changed — the loop's own notion of "prefix changed". The request/header events record epoch changes with reason initial/resume/change/series.
- Memories: none built-in; opt-in via external MCP memory servers; personas; skills; time-context opt-in injections as system-reminder user messages that get superseded ("Current runtime context: none. Earlier runtime-context snapshots no longer apply.").
- Goals: DSH has goals (dsh-goal) that persist in the session log; after session resume, an active goal is disarmed until the user asks to continue (this is in my system prompt!). Good parallel to Ultimate's automations/goal that keep working across restarts because the host stays alive.

Also worth checking quickly: does DSH web UI keep sessions "open" while the server runs — yes, live agents are reused on claim. The user's question is about "when I return to dsh and resume a session" — i.e., the session was closed/idle, server may have restarted; resume reloads the log.

One more Ultimate piece: what does the user see when they return to Ultimate? The splash extension says the splash stays until the app is back (`resumed`). The persistent chat: conversations are always in the sidebar; no explicit "resume" action needed — you just keep typing; if the host restarted, runs resume from last checkpoint. Concluded conversations get resumed automatically when input arrives ("The next input recreates a released checkout... resume... in the commit that places the input").

Also the tokens estimate: lineage catch-up ~6000 tokens cap. Memory brief = index + last 10 landings.

I should also verify DSH's web "resume" UX: sessions list, and that opening a session from the sidebar triggers claim/resume. And the session-stats package probably shows cache read/write tokens in the stats UI (dsh-experimental-client-ui-stats). Good enough.

Now let me also double check the DSH "memories" story: is there anything like CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md auto-load? There's dsh-agent-instructions and dsh-agent-preset (the AGENTS.md content — indeed my system prompt has "Current working directory", skills catalog etc.). Let me quickly check dsh-agent-instructions to describe how instructions/AGENTS.md are loaded into the system prompt on each turn (not stored per session).
I have most of both sides. Let me verify two last details: how DSH loads instructions (AGENTS.md) into context, and how Ultimate's host handles UI return/idle conversations.

Ultimate opens with its name: the ULTIMATE wordmark draws itself over the whole window while the app loads, and the
app comes up once the page is ready.

## What it does

- **On load** a root overlay covers the window until `useReady().ready`: every enabled facet has loaded or failed and
  the first system snapshot is in, or the core's 8 s deadline has passed. The shell holds the app itself back until
  then, so the overlay draws over the background `web/index.html` paints and nothing of the app flashes, however late
  the splash installs.
- **The show** (Web Animations API and WebGL): lightning draws the name, sweeping across its outline from left to
  right; at the end it bursts from the middle, a ripple with a flash and a spray of arcs that fades into a steady
  electric outline until the overlay goes. The lightning is `electric.tsx`, adapted from React Bits' ElectricLogo on
  `ogl`, its click burst included. Still loading after that, a quiet rule draws out beneath the name.
  Once ready, a drawing still in progress finishes within a quarter second and the overlay fades into the app. It
  stays at least 0.7 s, so a warm start does not flash.
- **First run** (onboarding's `status` action reports `firstRun`): the signature version plays slower and in full,
  with the rule, then the name lifts away as the overlay fades into onboarding's page beneath, which is already open.
  Without the `onboarding` extension there is no first run.
- **Reduced motion** (`prefers-reduced-motion`) or no WebGL2: the solid wordmark, no lightning, then a quick fade.
- **Never stuck**: not ready after 8 s, the core reveals the app anyway, and a small notice names the extensions still
  loading (`useReady().pending`) and those that failed (`useReady().failed`), until they load or it is dismissed.
- **Once per page load**: mounted when the page is already ready (a very warm start), it shows nothing,
  and nothing after ready brings it back.
- **Fresh starts only**: a reload of a rendered page (a core restart, a switch to a new web bundle, F5) shows the previous
  page's view until the app is back (`resumed` from `@/sdk`), so the splash stays away.
- **Rehearsal**: `?splash` holds the splash on screen, automated browsers included, and a click replays it;
  `?splash=first` plays the first run's version. For polishing it on a preview instance.
- **Automated browsers** (`navigator.webdriver`, as in the agent's `browser` and `screenshot` tools): no show, so the
  first frame is the app.

====
11:A preview runs every agent on one model and spends tokens: seed it by prompting it as a user would. The `instance.model` setting (`"provider/id"`, project over user, default `openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol`) reaches the preview as `ULTIMATE_MODEL`. There it wins over everything else: the root's default model, agent definition pins (@ultimate, coordinators, the lander, subagents, automation runs) and `summaryModel`; thinking levels are clamped to what it supports, and an `openai-codex/` or `openai/` model runs on the fast tier. `"instance": { "model": null }` turns the override off, so a preview runs the configured models. `instance start` with `model` overrides the setting for that preview only: a `provider/id`, or `null` for the configured models. Provider logins are read from `~/.pi/agent`, never copied. No state is copied; a workspace preview follows its main checkout's project decision, as every linked worktree does. Each preview keeps its own SQLite storage and Vite cache.
21:Its `link` renderer turns Markdown links to loopback ports into chips: a dot, then the link text. A link to a running preview has a brand dot and shows that preview in the frame at the link's path and query, without the external-link dialog. A link to a preview that no longer runs has a grey dot, does nothing, and says "Not running" on hover. A link to a loopback port this server never ran a preview on, such as a dev server, stays a normal link. A link to this server's own port opens in place, at the link's path and query. On a page opened from elsewhere, a running preview with a `tailnet` address opens it in a new tab, since that page has no switcher to return from a frame; one without says "Only on this machine". Other links keep the default.

I've explored both sides — Ultimate's persistence stack (SQLite core, lineage, recall, keep-warm, dream, conversations extensions) and the running DSH 0.2.2-rc.5 checkout's session packages. Here's the comparison.

# Ultimate's persistent chat vs. returning to DSH and resuming

**The structural difference in one sentence:** Ultimate's chat lives in a database that a long-lived host keeps open, so "returning" is a no-op; DSH's chat lives in an event log that must be re-instantiated, so "resume" is a rebuild procedure.

## What each one actually is

- **Ultimate** is Pi's coding agent in a web UI, built on **Pi Durable**: the conversation, every tool call, and every subagent are committed to SQLite (`~/.ultimate/projects/<name>-<hash>/state.sqlite` + `trace.sqlite`) *before anything is shown* ([docs/durability.md](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/docs/durability.md)). The UI is a view over that DB; the host runs continuously and can even hot-swap its own core (`self` extension's replay-safe `restart`) while busy agents resume in the new process.
- **DSH** sessions are **event-sourced append-only logs** persisted as zstd-compressed JSONL with single-writer leases and format migrations v0→v4 (`dsh-session-persistence-jsonl`); SQLite appears only as a *query index* (`dsh-session-query-sqlite`) plus JSON storage domains. The session class itself says it plainly: *"Seeding with an existing event log replays/forks a session"* ([dsh-session/src/index.ts](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-session/src/index.ts)).

## What "coming back" means in each

**Ultimate: nothing happens.** Conversations are always in the sidebar; you just keep typing. Concluded branches auto-resume *in the commit that places the input*; if the host restarted, each interrupted run resumes from its last checkpoint — replay-safe tools rerun, others report "interrupted", and external effects are at-least-once tasks with idempotency keys. A reload of the browser page doesn't even show the splash: "a reload of a rendered page … shows the previous page's view until the app is back (`resumed` from `@/sdk`)" ([splash](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/splash/README.md)).

**DSH: an explicit rebuild pipeline** ([dsh-agent-loop/src/index.ts](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-loop/src/index.ts) `resume()`):
1. Open the stored session with a **write lease** (excludes concurrent resumes).
2. **Cold read the entire log**; if the last turn was interrupted, append synthetic closers (missing tool errors, `step/end`, `turn/end`) so the log is a valid conversation again.
3. Seed a fresh in-memory `Session` with the full stored log, then publish the agent with `source: 'resume'`.
4. The next request logs a `request/header` with `reason: 'resume'` — the durable "I'm back" marker.

A cold read is softened by the **projection cache**: durable per-session checkpoints so the fold replays a short tail instead of the whole log ("a row is possibly stale … but never wrong"; a version mismatch just discards it) ([dsh-session-projection-cache](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-projection-cache/src/index.ts)).

## Axis by axis

| | Ultimate persistent chat | DSH session resume |
|---|---|---|
| **Context load** | *Curated re-entry.* A new branch inherits a **memory brief** (memory index + last 10 landings + pointer to the full tally), not raw history. An idle conversation's next input gets a **"Meanwhile in #R's tree" catch-up note** (~6,000-token budget: new abstracts, landings, notes), so it learns what happened while it was away ([lineage](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/lineage/README.md)). | *Faithful replay.* The model-visible surface is rebuilt from the same events as before the break — same context, byte-for-byte semantics, no catch-up summarization. Only static inputs refresh: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md is re-read at baseline with digest-tracked incremental updates pushed to the inbox, and opt-in **time-context** snapshots re-inject the clock mid-history with supersession notices ("Earlier runtime-context snapshots no longer apply"). |
| **Compaction** | Harness compaction per conversation; the tally's `compact` keeps "the idea, principles, standing decisions and each conversation's id, prompt, outcome, divergence, commits and breadcrumbs". The dream extension dreams *before* compaction (automation: context above 70%) and rotates whole **chapters** (fresh SQLite DB seeded with memories, learned lines, a ≤12k-char handover, open todos) ([dream](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/dream/README.md)). | `compaction-basic`: automatic at **80%** of the context window, keeping a **16%** verbatim tail; the selected surface span is replaced by one summary node; also forced on provider-confirmed overflow, manual via `/compact` ([dsh-compaction](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-compaction/src/index.ts)). |
| **Memories** | **Built-in and layered:** `lineage.memory` (≤150 slugged decisions/facts/lessons with breadcrumb sources), injected as branch briefs; **recall** re-injects relevant memories mid-conversation before @ultimate's request when context is ≥20% full (classify-scored, ≤3 memories at p≥0.25); scheduled **memory review branches** fact-check and propose ops; dream prunes what no longer earns its place. | **None built-in.** Memory is opt-in via external MCP servers (Memorix / MCP Reference Memory / Engram reference configs in the [mcp-memory guide](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/docs/user/guide/mcp-memory.md)); otherwise "memory" is just static instructions (AGENTS.md, personas, skills). Nothing automatically distills a session into a store. |
| **Prompt cache** | **A first-class, engineered concern.** Conversation-identity prompt text is deliberately immutable ("its text never changes, because every system prompt change costs the prompt cache"); recall injects "at the same position … which keeps the cached prompt prefix"; the pi-claude-code patch rebuilds cache markers within Claude's four-block limit and adopted the inline-tools beta after the merged-prompt fallback "rewrote @ultimate's whole cache (17 rewrites, 5.8M tokens in one day)"; **keep-warm pings every ~55–60 min** to renew Claude's 1-hour cache while you're away; the context extension even renders amber "cache rebuilt" lines explaining why ([pi-upstream.md](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/docs/pi-upstream.md), [keep-warm](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/keep-warm/README.md)). | **Metered and correctness-checked, but not kept warm.** The token meter records `cacheReadTokens`/`cacheWriteTokens` per turn; `request/header` epochs + `startsSeries` durably mark when the prefix changed; **prefix-binding digests** protect Anthropic signed thinking across compaction/pruning (stale signed blocks are dropped so requests stay valid) ([prefix-binding.ts](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-pi-ai/src/prefix-binding.ts)). But nothing renews a cache across an idle hour, and no UI narrates rebuilds. |
| **Crash semantics** | Run resumes from last checkpoint; interrupted tools declared replay-safe rerun (enforced by lint: `ultimate/replay-safe-by-name`), others report "interrupted"; every side effect is a durable task created in the same transaction as the decision. | Interrupted turn is *closed, not resumed*: synthetic closers make the log valid and the model sees honest tool errors; the checkpoint policy even **delays provider dispatch until the request prefix is durable** (`session-checkpoint-policy` flushes before the first stream chunk). |
| **Autonomy across the break** | Work keeps going: watchdog retries transient failures, automations fire on schedule, goals pin reminder notes — all stored in the same DB, so a restart continues them. | An active **goal is disarmed** after session resume; it only re-arms when you ask to continue. Queued work stays, but nothing self-starts on resume. |

## The deep difference

Both share the same durability philosophy — commit before you show (DSH flushes the request prefix before dispatching; Ultimate commits every entry before rendering) — and interestingly both ride on Pi lineage (DSH's LLM layer is `dsh-llm-pi-ai`; Ultimate patches `@earendil-works/pi-durable`). The divergence is *what the persistent unit is*:

- **Ultimate persists a living world.** The unit of persistence is a project's whole social graph — trees, tallies, memories, automations, dreams — in one writable SQLite brain. Returning means rejoining a world that kept existing without you; the cost it engineers against is **context drift and cache writes**.
- **DSH persists a faithful transcript.** The unit of persistence is one session's append-only log. Resuming means deterministically reconstructing exactly the context that existed before, with leases, crash repair, and projection checkpoints making the reconstruction cheap and safe; the cost it engineers against is **corruption, ambiguity, and invalid replay** (hence prefix digests and closers rather than warmth).

So: resuming in DSH gives you *the same conversation, perfectly preserved but cold* — same context, no new memories, cache write on the first turn after a long gap. Ultimate's persistent chat gives you *a conversation that aged while you were gone* — catch-up notes, refreshed memories, a warm cache if keep-warm was on, and mid-run work that never stopped.

# Ultimate's persistent chat vs. returning to DSH and resuming

**The structural difference in one sentence:** Ultimate's chat lives in a database that a long-lived host keeps open, so "returning" is a no-op; DSH's chat lives in an event log that must be re-instantiated, so "resume" is a rebuild procedure.

## What each one actually is

- **Ultimate** is Pi's coding agent in a web UI, built on **Pi Durable**: the conversation, every tool call, and every subagent are committed to SQLite (`~/.ultimate/projects/<name>-<hash>/state.sqlite` + `trace.sqlite`) *before anything is shown* ([docs/durability.md](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/docs/durability.md)). The UI is a view over that DB; the host runs continuously and can even hot-swap its own core (`self` extension's replay-safe `restart`) while busy agents resume in the new process.
- **DSH** sessions are **event-sourced append-only logs** persisted as zstd-compressed JSONL with single-writer leases and format migrations v0→v4 (`dsh-session-persistence-jsonl`); SQLite appears only as a *query index* (`dsh-session-query-sqlite`) plus JSON storage domains. The session class itself says it plainly: *"Seeding with an existing event log replays/forks a session"* ([dsh-session/src/index.ts](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-session/src/index.ts)).

## What "coming back" means in each

**Ultimate: nothing happens.** Conversations are always in the sidebar; you just keep typing. Concluded branches auto-resume *in the commit that places the input*; if the host restarted, each interrupted run resumes from its last checkpoint — replay-safe tools rerun, others report "interrupted", and external effects are at-least-once tasks with idempotency keys. A reload of the browser page doesn't even show the splash: "a reload of a rendered page … shows the previous page's view until the app is back (`resumed` from `@/sdk`)" ([splash](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/splash/README.md)).

**DSH: an explicit rebuild pipeline** ([dsh-agent-loop/src/index.ts](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-loop/src/index.ts) `resume()`):
1. Open the stored session with a **write lease** (excludes concurrent resumes).
2. **Cold read the entire log**; if the last turn was interrupted, append synthetic closers (missing tool errors, `step/end`, `turn/end`) so the log is a valid conversation again.
3. Seed a fresh in-memory `Session` with the full stored log, then publish the agent with `source: 'resume'`.
4. The next request logs a `request/header` with `reason: 'resume'` — the durable "I'm back" marker.

A cold read is softened by the **projection cache**: durable per-session checkpoints so the fold replays a short tail instead of the whole log ("a row is possibly stale … but never wrong"; a version mismatch just discards it) ([dsh-session-projection-cache](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-projection-cache/src/index.ts)).

| | Ultimate persistent chat | DSH session resume |
|---|---|---|
| **Context load** | *Curated re-entry.* A new branch inherits a **memory brief** (memory index + last 10 landings + pointer to the full tally), not raw history. Only static inputs refresh: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md is re-read at baseline with digest-tracked incremental updates pushed to the inbox, and opt-in **time-context** snapshots re-inject the clock mid-history with supersession notices ("Earlier runtime-context snapshots no longer apply"). |
| **Compaction** | Harness compaction per conversation; the tally's `compact` keeps "the idea, principles, standing decisions and each conversation's id, prompt, outcome, divergence, commits and breadcrumbs". The dream extension dreams *before* compaction (automation: context above 70%) and rotates whole **chapters** (fresh SQLite DB seeded with memories, learned lines, a ≤12k-char handover, open todos) ([dream](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/dream/README.md)). | `compaction-basic`: automatic at **80%** of the context window, keeping a **16%** verbatim tail; the selected surface span is replaced by one summary node; also forced on provider-confirmed overflow, manual via `/compact` ([dsh-compaction](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-compaction/src/index.ts)). |
| **Memories** | **Built-in and layered:** `lineage.memory` (≤150 slugged decisions/facts/lessons with breadcrumb sources), injected as branch briefs; **recall** re-injects relevant memories mid-conversation before @ultimate's request when context is ≥20% full (classify-scored, ≤3 memories at p≥0.25); scheduled **memory review branches** fact-check and propose ops; dream prunes what no longer earns its place. | **None built-in.** Memory is opt-in via external MCP servers (Memorix / MCP Reference Memory / Engram reference configs in the [mcp-memory guide](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/docs/user/guide/mcp-memory.md)); otherwise "memory" is just static instructions (AGENTS.md, personas, skills). Nothing automatically distills a session into a store. |
| **Prompt cache** | **A first-class, engineered concern.** Conversation-identity prompt text is deliberately immutable ("its text never changes, because every system prompt change costs the prompt cache"); recall injects "at the same position … which keeps the cached prompt prefix"; the pi-claude-code patch rebuilds cache markers within Claude's four-block limit and adopted the inline-tools beta after the merged-prompt fallback "rewrote @ultimate's whole cache (17 rewrites, 5.8M tokens in one day)"; **keep-warm pings every ~55–60 min** to renew Claude's 1-hour cache while you're away; the context extension even renders amber "cache rebuilt" lines explaining why ([pi-upstream.md](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/docs/pi-upstream.md), [keep-warm](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/extensions/keep-warm/README.md)). | **Metered and correctness-checked, but not kept warm.** The token meter records `cacheReadTokens`/`cacheWriteTokens` per turn; `request/header` epochs + `startsSeries` durably mark when the prefix changed; **prefix-binding digests** protect Anthropic signed thinking across compaction/pruning (stale signed blocks are dropped so requests stay valid) ([prefix-binding.ts](/opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-pi-ai/src/prefix-binding.ts)). But nothing renews a cache across an idle hour, and no UI narrates rebuilds. |
| **Crash semantics** | Run resumes from last checkpoint; interrupted tools declared replay-safe rerun (enforced by lint: `ultimate/replay-safe-by-name`), others report "interrupted"; every side effect is a durable task created in the same transaction as the decision. | Interrupted turn is *closed, not resumed*: synthetic closers make the log valid and the model sees honest tool errors; the checkpoint policy even **delays provider dispatch until the request prefix is durable** (`session-checkpoint-policy` flushes before the first stream chunk). |

Queued work stays, but nothing self-starts on resume. |

## The deep difference

Both share the same durability philosophy — commit before you show (DSH flushes the request prefix before dispatching; Ultimate commits every entry before rendering) — and interestingly both ride on Pi lineage (DSH's LLM layer is `dsh-llm-pi-ai`; Ultimate patches `@earendil-works/pi-durable`). The divergence is *what the persistent unit is*:

- **Ultimate persists a living world.** The unit of persistence is a project's whole social graph — trees, tallies, memories, automations, dreams — in one writable SQLite brain. Returning means rejoining a world that kept existing without you; the cost it engineers against is **context drift and cache writes**.
- **DSH persists a faithful transcript.** The unit of persistence is one session's append-only log. Resuming means deterministically reconstructing exactly the context that existed before, with leases, crash repair, and projection checkpoints making the reconstruction cheap and safe; the cost it engineers against is **corruption, ambiguity, and invalid replay** (hence prefix digests and closers rather than warmth).

So: resuming in DSH gives you *the same conversation, perfectly preserved but cold* — same context, no new memories, cache write on the first turn after a long gap. Ultimate's persistent chat gives you *a conversation that aged while you were gone* — catch-up notes, refreshed memories, a warm cache if keep-warm was on, and mid-run work that never stopped.

They want a bottom-line comparison of token cost when resuming. Let me reason from the evidence I gathered:

**DSH resume token cost:**
- Full log replay into memory (that's compute, not tokens).
- Token cost = next request's input tokens. The context is the same as before the break. If the provider prompt cache is still warm (e.g., DeepSeek's context caching, Anthropic 5-min/1h TTL), a resume shortly after reads cache at ~0.1x. If you return after the cache expired (typical case: you closed the app, come back hours later), the first request re-writes/reads the entire context fresh — full input price.
- DSH does nothing to keep the cache warm or to reduce context on resume. No catch-up summarization. So cost = full context at full price (or cache-write premium on Anthropic if cache_control writes; on DeepSeek, cache hits are cheaper, misses are full price).

**Ultimate resume token cost:**
- The host likely never stopped; keep-warm pings renew the cache during idle gaps (for Claude paths). So returning after <1h+ gaps costs a cache read (~1/10th input price). Keep-warm itself spends a tiny ping each ~hour (reads cached prefix — cache read cost, plus one output token "ok").
- If the gap exceeds the warm window, keep-warm deliberately doesn't ping (cold cache can't be renewed without rewriting), so next message rewrites the whole context — same as DSH.
- But Ultimate also has machinery to reduce the eventual context: branches start from memory briefs instead of full tally; compaction; dream chapters rotate DBs and keep context lean. And @ultimate's own conversation keeps growing though.
- Cost of Ultimate's extras: summary model calls (titles, abstracts, reply summaries — GPT-6 Luna by default, small model), keep-warm pings, recall classify calls (TypeSafe), memory review branches, dream branches. Those are extra token spends DSH doesn't incur. But per *resume* specifically, Ultimate's first real message is likely much cheaper if keep-warm kept the cache warm; otherwise roughly the same as DSH for the main conversation.

So bottom line: 
- Per-resume marginal cost of the main conversation: Ultimate usually cheaper (warm cache read ≈ 10% of input) vs DSH (cold full-price rewrite) whenever the return gap is under ~1h (or whenever keep-warm kept renewing). For gaps beyond an hour, roughly equal — both pay full context rewrite, and Ultimate might even cost slightly more because @ultimate's context tends to be huge (~550k tokens example given in keep-warm README: ~1.1M input-equivalent rewrite vs ~55k read).
- Whole-system accounting: Ultimate spends more tokens overall on maintenance (summary model, pings, classify, dream/review branches) — but those are diffuse background costs, not the resume event itself.

Also note provider matters: DeepSeek's automatic context caching (disk-based, no TTL like Anthropic's? DeepSeek context caching is automatic with no explicit TTL charge model; cache hits billed much less). Actually in this fictional 2026 world, providers differ; keep it general: provider-side cache TTLs determine whether DSH's first request after return hits. Anthropic-style TTL 5min default/1h optional; keep-warm targets the 1h one.

Bottom line answer should be crisp: 
- **If you're gone under ~an hour: Ultimate is far cheaper (~10x less on the first message) because keep-warm holds the cache; DSH pays the full rewrite.**
- **If you're gone for hours/days: it's a wash on the main message — both rewrite the full context at full price — and Ultimate's total bill runs higher because of its background maintenance spend (summarizer, pings stop when cold, classify, dream), though its branch/brief design can keep *contexts themselves* smaller over time.**

Also caveat: on DSH, resume itself is local compute (replay), zero tokens; the cost lands on the first message. Same for Ultimate.

**Bottom line: DSH. Resuming in DSH is the expensive one; Ultimate usually makes the return trip cheap — and for long absences they converge, with Ultimate costing more in the background.**

- **Away for minutes to ~an hour:** Ultimate wins big. keep-warm pings renew the prompt cache while you're gone, so your first message back reads it at roughly **1/10th input price** (the keep-warm README's own math: ~55k tokens-equivalent read vs ~1.1M rewrite at a ~550k-token context). DSH does nothing across the gap, so the same return re-writes the whole context at full price.

- **Away for hours or days:** roughly a **wash**. keep-warm deliberately doesn't ping a cache that's already cold, so Ultimate's first message back rewrites the full context just like DSH's does. (Ultimate's @ultimate conversation also tends to run huge, so its cold rewrite can be *bigger* in absolute terms — but its brief/branch design keeps individual work conversations smaller, which can offset that.)

DSH's resume is free locally (log replay is compute, not tokens); the entire cost lands on your first message.

One-line rule of thumb: **short returns → Ultimate is ~10× cheaper; long returns → same first-message cost, Ultimate quietly spends more around it.** The exact ratio depends on the provider's cache pricing/TTL (keep-warm is tuned for Claude's 1-hour TTL; a provider with always-on cheap prefix caching would shrink DSH's penalty too).

Run an on-demand second Ultimate to test core changes before restarting the shared host, or, in another project, to check that project's `.ultimate/` extensions. Start it, check its API and UI, then stop it. Creating a conversation never starts a preview automatically.

`instance` supports start, stop, logs and list. An isolated caller previews its ready workspace; `start {subagent: <child id>}` selects an owned child's workspace. A shared caller previews the host source and project. When the project is Ultimate itself, a workspace preview runs the workspace's own source and requires `server/main.ts` and `node_modules`; run `pnpm install` first. In any other project the host's Ultimate runs with the workspace as its project, and the prompt says the preview is not the project's own app. Previews do not prevent landing or removal.

A preview of a git project lands on its own branch, `ultimate/<hash>-preview` (the hash of its home, like its workspace branches), created at the project's tip, and never pushes, whatever `lander.push` says: its workspaces target that branch (`ULTIMATE_PREVIEW_BRANCH`). Its git processes also include `<home>/preview.gitconfig` in the previewed repository only (`includeIf gitdir:`): every push there is rewritten to a transport that does not exist, and a reference-transaction hook refuses changes to any branch or tag outside the preview's own `ultimate/<hash>-` branches. Stop and the sweep delete those branches with the home.

Start uses a temporary home unless a separate home is supplied. A preview cannot share the host's home or another running preview's home. The child binds to localhost port zero; the tool reads its `Ultimate: <URL>` stdout line and checks `/api/models`. Startup has a 60-second deadline, with the output tail included in errors.

A preview runs `server/main.ts` without the supervisor, so it cannot restart: verify restart and chapter-switch flows on a supervised scratch server instead (`ULTIMATE_HOME=$H ULTIMATE_USER_HOME=$H/user pnpm start --port <free port> --no-open` on a fresh `H=$(mktemp -d)`, see `docs/running.md`), and delete its home afterwards. A state no server can reach is reported as unverified, never faked by injecting entries.

A preview runs every agent on one model and spends tokens: seed it by prompting it as a user would. The `instance.model` setting (`"provider/id"`, project over user, default `openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol`) reaches the preview as `ULTIMATE_MODEL`. There it wins over everything else: the root's default model, agent definition pins (@ultimate, coordinators, the lander, subagents, automation runs) and `summaryModel`; thinking levels are clamped to what it supports, and an `openai-codex/` or `openai/` model runs on the fast tier. `"instance": { "model": null }` turns the override off, so a preview runs the configured models. `instance start` with `model` overrides the setting for that preview only: a `provider/id`, or `null` for the configured models. Provider logins are read from `~/.pi/agent`, never copied. No state is copied; a workspace preview follows its main checkout's project decision, as every linked worktree does. Each preview keeps its own SQLite storage and Vite cache.

Logs returns the last 200 lines; list shows running instances. At most three may run, including starts in progress; shutdown stops them all. Logs are available until stop. After the child exits, stop and host shutdown remove tool-created temporary homes, their registered Git worktrees (including dirty preview scratch) and workspace branches named with that preview home's hash. Any foreign branch checked out in a preview is preserved. An explicitly supplied `home` is preserved, including its worktrees and branches, for reuse or inspection.

On open, a background sweep removes dead `ultimate-instance-*` homes in the system temporary directory; failures become notices. Every host sweeps that shared directory, so a sweep runs only while it holds `ultimate-preview-sweep.lock.db` there and is skipped while another sweep does. It probes exclusive transactions on both `storage.lock.db` and `ultimate.lock.db`, holding them through cleanup, and preserves any home with a live PID sidecar. A parent PID lease protects a preview from publication until stop, including startup before the child acquires storage. SQLite locks protect live owners even when a sidecar is missing; malformed sidecars fail closed. No live preview is signalled or removed, including previews of another host. The tool is not replay-safe. Returned URLs work with screenshot or browser.

Each instance records the conversation it previews (or that started it in the shared checkout). The `list` action (`POST /api/extensions/instance/actions/list`) returns the ones that served their UI as `{ id, url, conversationId, running, tailnet? }`: running ones, and those that exited or were stopped (`running: false`). Stopped ones are kept per port in the home's `previews.json`, the last 50, so they survive the restart that stops every preview; a start that never became ready is not among them. `tailnet` is `https://<dns>:<port>` for a running preview that publishes itself there: a preview's own `tailscale` extension records its HTTPS port in `~/.ultimate/tailscale.json` under an owner token starting with its pid, and the DNS name is the host's (the `tailscale` service's status). Without the host's tailscale ready, or that entry, it is absent.

`web.tsx` renders instance cards with URL, pid and home, plus collapsible logs; the URL behaves as a preview link, and the card's dot and status turn grey once the preview is gone. It asks for `list` every 5 s, on every page, for the switcher (running previews only) and preview links. While previews run, a chip after the title bar's project chip is the switcher (`2 previews ▾`, just `▾` on phones, through `titlebar.left`), leaving `titlebar.project` to other extensions; it lists "This project" and each preview as `#<conversation> <title>  :<port>`; opening it asks again. Choosing a preview shows its whole UI in a frame below the title bar, which the embedded page leaves out, and the chip names it (`● #12 · :41234 ▾`). "This project", another surface, or the preview stopping returns to this project; a reload does too. Pages opened from elsewhere than loopback, such as the tailnet, show no switcher, since the frame needs loopback URLs.

Its `link` renderer turns Markdown links to loopback ports into chips: a dot, then the link text. A link to a running preview has a brand dot and shows that preview in the frame at the link's path and query, without the external-link dialog. A link to a preview that no longer runs has a grey dot, does nothing, and says "Not running" on hover. A link to a loopback port this server never ran a preview on, such as a dev server, stays a normal link. A link to this server's own port opens in place, at the link's path and query. On a page opened from elsewhere, a running preview with a `tailnet` address opens it in a new tab, since that page has no switcher to return from a frame; one without says "Only on this machine". Other links keep the default.

content.text:
A project switcher at the window's left edge: every Ultimate running on this machine, one click away.

## How it works

- **Rail** (`shell.rail`, on desktop and tablet; nothing on a phone): one row per running instance, in project order. It shows only while at least two projects run.
  - Collapsed, the rail is one quiet column of colour, a swatch per project and no letters (`ProjectSwatch` from the sidebar). Ultimate's own family (`ultimate`, `ultimate-eval`, a branch checkout of it) is the brand purple; every other project takes a muted, cool hue (sage, teal, blue; no warm hues, so nothing reads as amber or red, and no violet, which stays Ultimate's), derived from the folder name alone (`colourOf` in the sidebar's `tile.tsx`, small and exported for other overviews), so a project keeps its colour on every instance and in the sidebar's header. Projects sharing a name stem (`ultimate`, `ultimate-eval`, `ultimate-fleet`) take neighbouring shades of one hue, and their adjacent swatches join into one strip with a gap before the next family. Other projects' swatches are slightly faded until hovered; the one this page shows is wider and full colour, ringed, with a brand bar on the edge. The swatch, its amber count and its working dot share the column's vertical axis.
  - Hovering opens it over the app (272 px); the pin button keeps it open beside the app. Each row then shows the display name (`prettyName`), and under it the GitHub `owner/repo` with a lock when private, and the port. The pin is one value for every instance on this machine (`~/.ultimate/projects-rail.json`), so jumping keeps the rail as it was.
  - On a page opened over the tailnet a row goes to the host the page came from, on that project's Tailscale port (`tailnetPort`, from the registry `~/.ultimate/tailscale.json`), since a loopback address means nothing there. A project not published on the tailnet shows dimmed, with no link. `links.ts` decides both from the page's host.
  - A row is a plain link to the instance's `/`, which opens its @ultimate: a click goes there in this tab, mod-click or middle-click opens a new tab, Back returns. The old page stays until the new one paints (seconds while the target builds its web bundle), so a click pulses its swatch, says "opening…" and runs a thin brand bar along the window's top; a page restored by Back clears it.
  - Live state, polled every 4 s while the tab is visible: an amber count of questions waiting for the user, else a pulsing brand dot while an agent works (questions outrank working; the two never show together). Folded, they sit on the swatch: amber is the only warm colour in the column, so a project waiting on you stands out. The footer sums it up (`1 for you · 2 working`).
- **Another rail wins:** when any other enabled extension fills `shell.rail` (a fleet switcher of your own, say), this one renders nothing and stops polling, so the window never shows two rails.

## Files

- `server.ts`
  - `list`, `{}` → `RunningProject[]` (`refs.ts`): the projects `host.projects()` finds running (their supervisor lock is held by a live process), each with its loopback URL; a branch checkout's name is `<project> #<id>`, so it shows and colours with its project. Each carries its `origin`'s GitHub `repo` (`{name, url, visibility?}`) once known: read in the background on first sight (`git`, then one `gh repo view`) and kept for the process, so a poll never waits on it. This instance's `busy` and `questions` come from its own conversations and open questions; every other instance's from its `status` action over loopback, waiting at most 1.5 s. One that does not answer in time is listed without them.
  - `pin`, `{ pinned? }` → `{ pinned }`: the shared pin, written first when `pinned` is given.
- `web.tsx`: the rail and the opening bar.
=====

commands.md
contracts.md

example-app.md

## Running the server

- `pnpm install`, then `pnpm start` runs the supervisor on Node 26. It owns the public TCP port and single-instance lock, prints the URL and opens it as a Chrome app window (`http://ultimate.localhost:<port>`, a tab without a Chrome-family browser; on macOS the installed Chrome app of that origin, found by its `CrAppModeShortcutURL` in `~/Applications/Chrome Apps.localized`, when there is one); `--no-open` or `ULTIMATE_NO_OPEN=1` disables opening.
- Run `pnpm add -g "$PWD"` once in the clone, then `cd ~/Projects/app && ultimate`. `ultimate [dir] [--port N] [--no-open]` starts in that project, or opens a window of it when it already runs; `pnpm start` in the clone uses the clone as the project.
- Project config belongs in `<project>/.ultimate/`: extensions, agents, skills, and optional `settings.json` (JSON object; `defaultSurface` selects the preferred surface). Discovery is built-in, user `~/.ultimate/`, then project config; later names win. User config is independent of `ULTIMATE_HOME`.
- Server facets can export `actions`, a map of async `(args, ctx)` functions callable from codemode with `ultimate.action(extension, action, args?)` or from the UI by `POST /api/extensions/:name/actions/:action` with `{ args, conversationId? }`, returning `{ result }`. `ctx` has `host`, optional `conversationId`, `signal`, and `exec(command, args, { cwd?, timeout? })`; exec uses the project cwd, no shell, a 1 MiB output cap and a maximum 30 second timeout.
- `pnpm dev` runs the core standalone; the `restart` tool requires `pnpm start`.
- The browser gets a production bundle of `web/` and every enabled `web.tsx` (`server/web.ts`), built by `server/web-build.ts` in a child process into `<home>/web/<id>/` and served precompressed; the bundler's memory goes when that child exits. While a page is open, a change to a bundled source rebuilds it about 150 ms later (a build takes about 2 s) and the page reloads onto the new `system.web.id`, resuming its view and drafts (`web/src/sdk/resume.ts`). With no page open a change only marks the bundle stale, and the next page load builds it. A `web.tsx` that does not build is left out: its loader rejects with the build error, so its error card shows while the rest runs, and a notice names the file; any other build failure keeps the previous bundle and raises a notice. In the server process Vite only loads server facets (`ssrLoadModule`) and watches files: no browser dependency optimizing, no HMR socket.
- Call `restart` after editing `server/` or `shared/`, or after a landing that changed `patches/` or `pnpm-lock.yaml`, never for `web/`, `extensions/`, or `agents/`. `POST /api/restart` accepts the same swap; reconnect to events to observe the new generation. The supervisor type-checks and prepares a new child without storage, then waits for the old harness to close before opening the new one and resuming work. Failed checks/preparation keep the old child serving.
- A crashed child restarts with backoff. After three failed boots the supervisor serves diagnostics and retries on changes in `server/`, `shared/`, or `extensions/`.
- With Tailscale enabled, the server logs its HTTPS URL as `Ultimate: https://… (remote)` when Tailscale registers it (usually after startup), and logs again when it is no longer served; under the supervisor these are core log lines. The interactive dashboard also keeps the current remote URL at its top, with the local URL underneath, and updates it when remote access changes.
- Binds only `127.0.0.1`; `--port`, then `ULTIMATE_PORT`, then the project's `.ultimate/settings.json` `port` fix the port (taken, the start fails), otherwise the supervisor chooses the first free port from `4747`.
- `ULTIMATE_HOME` overrides state storage; the default is `~/.ultimate/projects/<basename>-<sha256(projectRoot) first 8 hex>/`. Different projects can run concurrently, each its own dedicated process, so one Ultimate can manage the others (see [One Ultimate or many](../README.md#one-ultimate-or-many)). Never run two storage owners on the same home.
- `ULTIMATE_GENERATION` defaults to `1` and labels the process in system info.
- Pi's models, settings, and auth are shared with `~/.pi/agent`; the `models` extension logs in to providers.
- `pnpm check` checks format/lint/types; `pnpm test` runs the fast in-process tests with temporary homes (about 60 s today), each scripting its model responses on Pi's faux provider (`prepareHarness({ faux })`, test-only); `pnpm test:e2e` runs the `test/e2e` folders, the tests that spawn real supervisors and instances, on a scripted OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`test/e2e/scripted-model.ts`). The core's and integration tests are in `test/`, each extension's in `extensions/<name>/test/`; pass a path to run a part (`pnpm test extensions/<name>/`). Test servers find no Tailscale CLI (`TAILSCALE_COMMAND`), so they stay off the tailnet.
- UI and behaviour are verified on a preview: `instance start` runs a clean Ultimate with every agent on `instance.model` (default `openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol`, fast; its own home; provider logins are read from `~/.pi/agent`, never copied). Its user config is a private copy in `<home>/user/.ultimate` (`ULTIMATE_USER_HOME`), taken at start with links resolved: settings, model families, agents, skills, trust, onboarding and secrets, so a preview's clicks never change the real `~/.ultimate`; user `extensions/` and the Tailscale registry stay shared through links. Seed it by prompting it as a user would, then look with screenshot or browser (the `verify-ui` skill has the checklist). It spends tokens; stop it when done.
- Restart and chapter-switch flows need a supervised scratch server, since a preview runs `server/main.ts` without the
  supervisor and cannot restart. From the checkout under test, with the host's variables cleared (an agent's shell
  inherits the live server's `ULTIMATE_*`), on an empty user home so the real user extensions in `~/.ultimate` do
  not load into it:
  `H=$(mktemp -d); env $(env | grep -o '^ULTIMATE_[A-Z_]*' | sed 's/^/-u /') ULTIMATE_HOME=$H ULTIMATE_USER_HOME=$H/user pnpm start --port 4799 --no-open`.
  The home must be its own: never the project's default home, which is the live server's. Tailscale follows user
  settings, so with it on there the scratch server publishes on its own tailnet port (`https://<machine>:4799`,
  registered under the scratch home) for the user to open remotely, and frees only that port when it stops; the live
  server's address is untouched. Stop it and delete the scratch home when done.
  A state you cannot reach is reported as unverified, never faked by injecting entries.
- `tsconfig.swap.json` is the server-only type-check gate for swaps.
- `tsconfig.json` (server, tests, tooling) references `tsconfig.web.json` (browser: `web/src`, `extensions/**/*.tsx`).
  `pnpm check` type-checks both; with plain `tsc`, run `tsc -b`.
- The standalone server shuts down on SIGINT/SIGTERM; reopening resumes durable work. A supervised core ignores both
  and logs a warning: the supervisor stops it over IPC, so such a signal either reached the whole group while the
  service stops Ultimate, or came from outside (an agent's kill by port or name). Stop Ultimate through the supervisor (`pnpm start`'s process, or its service).
- Closing a server runs the extensions' release callbacks, then closes the Harness before disposing them, so work running at shutdown stays pending and resumes
  on the next open instead of faulting on a disposed extension.

## Starting fresh

`pnpm reset [dir] [--dry-run] [--yes]` starts a project's Ultimate from an empty state. It deletes nothing: `state.sqlite`, `trace.sqlite`, parked `state.stale-*` databases (each with its
`-wal`/`-shm`), every later chapter (`chapters/`, `chapters.json`, `pending-chapter.json`), `conversations.json`,
`previews.json` and `supervisor.log` move to
`~/.ultimate/backups/reset-<time>/<home>/`, and it prints that folder and the `mv` that restores it.

- Stop Ultimate first (`systemctl --user stop ultimate`); it refuses while the
  home's `ultimate.lock` or `storage.lock` is held, and holds both while it moves files.
- Kept: settings, secrets, logins, `project.json`, the lander checkout, worktrees and `ultimate/*` branches. It lists
  worktrees with uncommitted changes and branches not merged into the project's HEAD.
- It journals its progress in `<home>/reset.json`: an interrupted reset finishes into the same backup when run again,
  and `ultimate` refuses to start while the journal exists. `pnpm restore` uses the same journal
  (`extensions/cloud/README.md`).

`pnpm restore [name|key]` is its counterpart for cloud backups: it moves the same files into
`~/.ultimate/backups/restore-<time>/<home>/` and installs a backup in their place (see "Cloud backups" in
`extensions/cloud/README.md`).

content.text:
159:### One Ultimate or many
160-
161-Ultimate works both ways. Start it in one project and use it as an individual agent. Or run several: each project
162-is its own dedicated Ultimate process, on one machine or across several, and one Ultimate manages the others. It
163-reads their conversations, messages their @ultimate and watches their status; for example, a hub project whose
164-@ultimate checks the other projects and starts work in them. That is why every project gets its own process and
165-state home instead of one server for all of them.
166-
167-The building blocks that make it possible:
168-
169-- **Finding each other:** on one machine, every running instance shows up with its URL in `ultimate.projects()`
170-  and answers over loopback; no Tailscale needed. Across machines, list each instance in the `remotes` user setting,
171-  `{ "<machine>": { "<project>": "<url>" } }` ([Discovery and settings](docs/settings.md)).
172-- **Reading:** codemode's `ultimate.conversations`, `entries`, `search`, `trace` and `doc` take `{ project }` and
173-  read another running instance read-only ([Codemode](extensions/codemode/README.md#other-projects)).
174-- **Messaging:** `ultimate.tell({ project, text })` messages another project's @ultimate, and its answer comes back
175-  as a reply ([Messages](extensions/messages/README.md#other-projects-ultimates)).
176-- **Watching:** the `status` action reports an instance's health, failures and extensions in one cheap call
177-  ([Status](extensions/status/README.md)).
178-- **Reaching other machines:** the [Tailscale](extensions/tailscale/README.md) extension serves each instance on
179-  your tailnet, to your own login only.
180-
181-## Building blocks
182-
183-Built-ins live in the clone's `extensions/`; each folder's README describes the building block. Most are on by
184-default, a few (such as `cloud`, `parallel` and `tailscale`) start off, and the core tier is always on. Switch them in
185-`~/.ultimate/settings.json` for this machine or `<project>/.ultimate/settings.json` for this project; see
186-[discovery and settings](docs/settings.md) for the list, precedence, project trust and live updates.
187-
188-## Surfaces
189-
190-A surface is a full-screen app made of extensions: the **Agent** surface is the conversation you start with; another
191-can be anything you build. Switch in the title bar, `⌘K` → "Switch to …", or `mod+1…9`. The agent
192-stays docked on every surface, and the choice is durable: reloads, other tabs, and restarts land on the same view.
193-`documents` provides the Documents tab; surface UI contributions themselves work without it.
194-
195-## What to try
196-
197-- Start a new project with **Set up with @ultimate** on the Start here card in @ultimate's conversation (or Continue on the first-run Get ready page).
198-  Choose setup on the inline cards, steer its reading, then start your first coordinator branch from the project's context.
199-- Ask it anything about this repository; watch tool calls, diffs, and thinking stream in.

content.text:
# Server facets: host, lifecycle, tools and prompt

Part of the [extension guide](../../extensions/README.md).

`server.ts` exports a Pi Durable extension, `defineExtension({ name })` with the folder's name, or a factory
receiving the `ExtensionHost` below. See `prompt/` for prompt sections and `coding-tools/server.ts` for tools; the
root `AGENTS.md` explains reloads and durability. Local imported modules reload with the facet; a failed load leaves
the previous version installed. Besides the extension it may export `docs` ([documents](documents.md)), `actions`,
`userActions` and `pollActions` ([actions](actions.md)), `secrets` ([secrets](places.md#secrets)),
`reloadOnSettings` (below) and `order`.

## Order and prompt sections

Server facets may `export const order = -100`: lower values come first, with the default 0 keeping discovery order
(built-in → user → project, then folder name); changing it reorders the server prompt and tools once.

Prompt sections stay stable between turns: the same conversation renders the same text every time, so the prompt
stays cached. Anything that changes while a conversation runs (a count, a list, a time) goes in a per-input note
from a `beforeInput` hook instead. For example, `todos/server.ts` does not list open to-dos in a section; its
`beforeInput` returns a note only when the list changed since the conversation last saw it.

## Extension host

Server factories receive exactly these `ExtensionHost` fields (import its type only from `server/extensions.ts`):

- `ultimateRoot`, `projectRoot`, `userHome`, `home`: source, work, user and instance-state roots.
- `modelRuntime`, `settings`: Pi model/auth runtime and settings.
- `models()`: model descriptors, including availability.
- `skills(cwd)`: merged clone, user and project skills for a working directory, each with its `scope` and `overrides`.
- `restart(approved)`: request a verified core swap; the async callback records the approved generation before activation.
- `scanSubmissions(query, limit, cursor, caller)`: a page of committed submission records; it exists until Pi Durable exposes submission scans publicly.
- `chapter`: the active chapter: its name, number, the newest chapter's name and its files.
- `build()`, `system()`, `extensions()`: current build, system and extension inspection.
- `conversations()`: every conversation's summary, as `useConversations()` gives the web; empty until the harness is open.
- `projects()`: the user's central project homes read from their JSON manifests, never another project's SQLite; includes this home and live supervisor URLs.
- `projectSetup()`: whether the project has `.ultimate/` setup, the decision of its root (a linked worktree's main checkout) and its capped README.
- `projectSettings()`: the project's parsed settings, only after a local decision; otherwise empty.
- `projectExtensions()`: a read-only inventory of the project's extension folders, including replacements of active extensions.
- `setProjectDecision(local)`: remember the local/global choice and apply it through the live settings reload.
- `reloadExtensions()`: apply settings writes to the registry, browser facets and styles before returning.
- `invoke(name, action, args, signal, conversationId?)`: call an installed extension action on behalf of a conversation; rejects user-only actions.
- `harness()`, `uiState(context)`, `doc(kind)`: durable harness, root UI snapshot and exported conversation document token.
- `implement(api, value)`, `need(api)`, `want(api)`, `catalogue()`: publish and use typed process-local services; see [contracts](contracts.md). Registrations are staged until installation succeeds, replaced on reload, and removed when the facet is disabled, removed or closed; a failed replacement keeps the old provider.
- `metadata`: the core's `ultimate.metadata` conversation document, `{ title?, label? }`; the shell names a conversation
  by them, so set them on conversations you create (`subagents` labels each child with its definition).
- `emit(tx, event, data)`, `react(name, events, handler)`, `eventLog`: durable events; see [events](events.md).
- `trace`: the recorded calls (services, actions, reactor runs, tools); see [tracing](introspection.md#tracing).
- `access.allow({ origin, verify })`: register an HTTP origin with an identity verifier; returns a disposer and is automatically removed when the facet unloads or reloads. HTTP, API, and websocket upgrades use the same admission rules.
- `notice(message, { untilSecretSet? })`: publish a warning notice and retain it in this facet's system diagnostics for later clients, until unload/reload. With `untilSecretSet: 'NAME'` the diagnostic is gone as soon as that secret is stored.
- `resource(key, create)`, `onOpen(callback)`, `onRelease(callback)`, `onClose(cleanup)`: shared reload-stable resources, async work each
  time the harness opens (at once if it is open; the server serves once it settles), async work each time before it closes while the process stays (a core swap; drop commit subscriptions there), and async cleanup. Facet-level callbacks are removed on unload/reload, with cleanup run before the replacement opens. Callbacks registered inside a shared resource's creation belong to that reload-stable resource and survive until server shutdown.
  Keep only process state in a resource (running children, in-flight promises, flags); never capture document or task
  tokens or facet functions in it, since they go stale on reload. Build those on each install around the shared state.
- `onLoadError(callback)`: run `callback(name, error)` each time an extension's server facet fails to load; facet-scoped.
- `onBeforeLoad(callback)`: run and await `callback()` before each extension reload, web build and restart, so none reads a checkout or packages still being written (`update` waits for git and installs owed packages there). When it throws, a reload or build goes on with a notice and a restart is refused with the message; facet-scoped.

## Lifecycle

Facet-registered `onOpen` and `onClose` callbacks are facet-scoped: they end on reload, disable, or unload. An `onOpen` registered after installation while the harness is already open runs immediately. Cleanup failures produce notices and do not stop the remaining facet cleanups. Callbacks registered synchronously inside a `resource()` factory are process-scoped and survive reloads until server shutdown. Process-scoped cleanups settle independently; failures produce notices without preventing core shutdown.

A server facet can export `reloadOnSettings = true` to reinstall on live settings changes even when its enablement is unchanged. Its scoped lifecycle callbacks and access registrations are cleaned up before its replacement opens.

Type imports from `server/` are fine. Runtime imports need a host capability or a visible lint exception.
====
# Core tier

Part of the [extension guide](../../extensions/README.md).

The core tier is the fixed heart of Ultimate that every other extension may rely on. An extension joins it with one
line in its `api.ts`, `export const tier = 'core'` (`coreTier` in `shared/extension-api.ts`); nothing in `server/`
names them. A user or project folder is core only when it replaces a core built-in of the same name. Discovery reads
the line: a core-tier extension stays enabled whatever `extensions.disable` says (the
ignored entry becomes an extension diagnostic), and `ExtensionInfo.core` marks it, so the first-run choices and the
Extensions panel show it as `core` with a locked switch. Being always on, a core-tier service is there for every
extension: consumers `need` it. `want` is for optional extensions' services and for extension points, which another
extension fills. `test/e2e/disable-each.test.ts` boots with each optional extension disabled in turn and expects a
clean catalogue.

Today's core tier: agent, prompt, coding-tools, entries, conversations, models, documents, notices, secrets, theme,
workspaces, subagents, lineage, messages, automations, onboarding (the first run and @ultimate's setup cards need it)
and sidebar.

Dependencies point one way. A core-tier extension imports (runtime or type), needs and wants only core-tier
extensions; lint's `core-tier-deps` enforces the imports, and the catalogue has no cycles. `pnpm deps`
(`scripts/deps.ts`, part of `pnpm check`) prints the graph between built-in extensions, from every import (runtime,
type, re-export, dynamic) and every `need`/`want` of another extension's token, and fails on a cycle or a core-tier
extension depending on an optional one. The core layers, lowest first, each depending only on layers below it:

1. prompt, coding-tools, documents, notices, secrets, theme, entries: stand alone. entries holds the entry kinds that
   extensions on both sides of a dependency read (`lineage.note`, `board.message`, `board.reply`,
   `automations.fired`), so the reader imports neither writer.
2. models.
3. conversations: titles, summaries, overview, concluding; `ConversationRef`, `FeatureTag`, `AgentMark`.
4. workspaces: worktrees and the lander.
5. subagents: child conversations and standing agents.
6. lineage: roots, branches, tallies, notes.
7. messages: delivery and the `branch` tool.
8. automations: schedules, scripts, events and context triggers that wake conversations.
9. onboarding and agent.
10. sidebar: the sidebar and the @ultimate button, the UI that brings the core together.

Where a lower extension needs something a higher one knows, it declares the contract and the higher one fills it:
server extension points (`conversations.trees` and `conversations.release` from conversations, `workspaces.branches`
from workspaces), web points (`conversations.phase`, `conversations.task`, `conversations.unsummarized`,

- Agent-facing tools (bash/fs/edit/web/etc.) → Ultimate tools (pi tools); but implementations differ (DSH tool executor/PTC runtime vs Pi's tool API).
- System-prompt contributions/instructions → prompt sections.

- Cordis Service/DI, Context events, config schemas (Schemastery/zod), loader patches (cordis.patch.yml), HMR receiver, the session event log API (dsh-session*), the LLM middleware chain (agent/request waterfall, pre-step decisions), token meter, sandbox policy/permission presets, approval answerers — Ultimate has its own equivalents but with totally different APIs (Pi Durable harness, transactions, documents, durable tasks).

# Persistent Harness plugins

A plugin change is a bundle: author its package in ordinary workspace files, then install it with `plugin_manager` `action: install_bundle` and the absolute package directory as `target`. Changes affect every session in the profile and survive restart. Read `references/compositions.md` for agent preset changes.

Do not write the profile's `package.json` or `cordis.patch.yml`, create packages under `$DSH_HOME`, or run pnpm in the profile directory: `install_bundle` performs those steps, and each hand-made write outside the workspace needs its own approval. Every `plugin_manager` action, including `list_plugins` and `list_bundles`, also needs approval without Full access, so call it only when its result decides the next step. When `plugin_manager` is not among your tools, finish the bundle in the workspace, then tell the user its directory and that **Plugins** > **Add plugin** installs a local directory; do not change a preset to gain the tool.

## Design or review

Read the applicable references and check the proposed or existing plugin against current APIs. Report design choices or findings. Do not write files, install bundles, or change profile state unless the user requests implementation.

## Enable a shipped plugin

A shipped bundle can resolve a plugin row and leave it `disabled`. The row id and its reason are in the shipped patch, `packages/bundle/*/cordis.patch.yml` in a source checkout. Write a workspace bundle whose patch overrides that row with `disabled: false` and inserts the Host rows it depends on; a source checkout's `apps/cli/config/examples/<feature>/cordis.yml` lists them for opt-in features. Packages shipped with dsh resolve from the dsh installation, so the bundle declares no dependencies on them. Install it with `install_bundle`.

## Deliver a working plugin first

1. Resolve the requested result and where it appears in DSH; when the place is unclear, ask. Choose reasonable details and implement a small first version; install it before visual refinement.
2. Discover only the APIs needed for that version. With inspection tools, call `cordis_inspect_list`, then targeted `cordis_inspect_query` calls; for UI, query Client `Slots.listSubTree` and the selected slot's registration options and props. Without them, read the owning package README and source as `references/locate-docs.md` describes, and report that live registration was not inspected. For anything beyond a static decoration, such as tool policy, agent context, session-derived state, or Chat rows, read `references/practices.md` before choosing the extension point; for a user action in plugin UI, also read `references/user-actions.md`.
3. Copy the matching template files into one workspace directory, or author the package, patch, and required Host/Client files there. Before installing, complete the display checklist in `references/host-plugin.md`: localized titles and descriptions, optional single-image details, an original or licensed icon, and exported resources with distribution checks where applicable. This applies to Host-only and configuration-only bundles too; adapt template text and artwork to the request. Check JavaScript syntax and the manifest, then install. Use the installed plugin as the first preview; do not create preview HTML, mock shells, design variants, screenshot scripts, or rasterizer tooling first.
4. Read the installation result; when the user installed the bundle, ask them to confirm its row in **Plugins**, verify in a new session, and report what remained unverified. `application` and `warnings` decide whether the change is live, not logs, process lists, or the page's boot payload. Confirm new rows with approval-free `cordis_inspect_query` when available, not `list_plugins`. After `application: applied`, exercise the capability or inspect the live Client registration. Verify installed display metadata and the icon using `references/host-plugin.md`, and any detail image using `references/plugin-details.md`. Use the connected page when available; follow `references/verification.md` for page and panel checks and unavailable browser control, and `references/user-actions.md` for user actions. Restore user state changed during testing. Report verification limits; installation and slot registration alone do not establish what the user sees.
5. For a new plugin or a change to its user experience, run the user experience review in `references/verification.md`.
6. Fix observed defects in the same plugin. When the requested result works, finish with its location, verification status, and the reason for any display-resource exception; never silently accept default artwork. Do not continue speculative variants, unrelated optional features, or mock HTML/page previews. The bundle's optional detail image follows `references/plugin-details.md`. Close any task list.

## Profile facts

`DSH_PROFILE` (profile name) and `DSH_PROFILE_DIR` (its directory, whose `node_modules` holds only profile-installed bundles) are set in every shell call of a profile-launched Harness and absent when the Harness was booted without a profile. Bash reads them as `$DSH_PROFILE`; PowerShell reads them as `$env:DSH_PROFILE`. With `dsh` on the PATH, `dsh --profile "$DSH_PROFILE" --dump-config` prints the composed profile. Bundled packages resolve from the dsh installation and profile-installed bundles from the profile, so never guess a package path from `$DSH_PROFILE_DIR`.

Connects the MCP servers in `mcpServers` and lets agents use their tools through one `mcp` tool; the status line shows how many are connected.

## Settings

`mcpServers` takes the same shape as Claude Desktop and Cursor, so a server's config pastes in. Put it in `~/.ultimate/settings.json`, or in a project's `.ultimate/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "files": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/path/to/folder"]
    },
    "my-server": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${MY_SERVER_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}
```

- **stdio:** `command`, optional `args`, `env` and `cwd` (default: the project root). The server inherits Ultimate's environment plus `env`.
- **Streamable HTTP:** `url` and optional `headers`. The legacy SSE transport is not supported.
- **Secrets:** `${NAME}` in `args`, `env`, `url` or `headers` is replaced by the secret `NAME` from the Secrets panel (⌘K → Secrets). Never write a token inline. Each such name is declared as a secret, so the Secrets panel lists it, set or missing, with the servers using it. A missing secret fails that server with its name and an Add button; saving it there connects the server again.
- **Precedence:** user and project servers merge by name; a project entry replaces a user entry of the same name. Project servers run commands, so they load only once the project's setup is trusted (`host.projectSettings()` is empty before).
- `"disabled": true` leaves a server out.

Saving either settings file reconnects every server. OAuth is not supported yet: a server behind OAuth needs a token or service credentials in headers.

## Tool

`mcp {server}` lists a server's tools with their input schemas; `mcp {server, tool, args}` calls one and returns its text and images. A result the server marks as an error comes back as a tool error. The tool's description names the configured servers, so the prompt changes only when the configuration does, however many tools they have. In codemode, `tools.mcp(...)` runs many calls and filters their results.

Every agent that inherits tools gets `mcp`, and @ultimate lists it in `agents/ultimate.md`. Agents with an explicit `tools` list add it there.

Calls are `replay: 'unsafe'`: a call interrupted by a restart is reported as interrupted, never sent again. A call times out after 10 minutes without progress from the server.

## Lifecycle

Servers connect when the server opens, each on its own: a failing one never blocks another or a turn. A failure or a dropped connection retries after 5 s, doubling up to 5 minutes. The servers close (stdio: the whole process group) when the extension reloads or Ultimate stops. A server's `tools/list_changed` notification refreshes its tool list.

## UI

The status line's `mcp 2/3` chip counts connected out of configured servers, turns red while one failed, and is hidden when none is configured. Its popover lists each server with its transport, source, state or tool count, the error and the next retry, and a reconnect button. The Extensions panel's `mcp` row lists the same servers when opened.

Actions: `status` → every server's state; `reconnect {name}` → connects one again and returns the states.

SKILL.md
---
name: write-extension
description: Build or change an Ultimate extension or surface (a panel, status-line item, tool or entry renderer, command, dialog, full-screen app, server tool or prompt section) in extensions/ or a project's .ultimate/extensions/. Use before writing a new extension folder or adding a contribution to one; not for small fixes inside an existing renderer.
---

# Write an Ultimate extension

`extensions/README.md` (in the Ultimate clone) is a short index; each topic is its own file in `docs/extensions/`.
Follow these steps and open only the topics named.

## 1. Place it

- A built-in Ultimate feature: `extensions/<name>/` in the clone.
- One project's tool or app: `<project>/.ultimate/extensions/<name>/` (in Ultimate's own repo that is
  `.ultimate/extensions/`, not `extensions/`).
- Personal, every project: `~/.ultimate/extensions/<name>/`.

The folder name is the extension name. New UI is a new folder, never a change to `web/`.

## 2. Copy the closest extension

Read the table at the top of `extensions/README.md` and open the extension it names for what you build
(`status-line`, `models`, `info`, `coding-tools`, `plan`, the Commits example in `docs/extensions/example-app.md`). Copy its shape; change the content.

## 3. Pick the facets

| File        | For                                                             | Goes live           |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `web.tsx`   | UI: `defineWebExtension({ slots, panels, surfaces, tools, … })` | Rebuilt on save     |
| `server.ts` | tools, prompt sections, hooks, documents, `actions`             | reinstalled on save |
====
# Contributions: slots and panels

Part of the [extension guide](../../extensions/README.md).

`defineWebExtension({ slots, panels, panelBadges, surfaces, tools, toolLines, entries, link, messageActions, messageDetails, answerLabels, userBubble, compact, documents, commands })`; every key is optional. Extensions load
in parallel, installing independently; contributions follow discovery order: built-in → user → project, then folder name within each source. Give a slot item `{ component, order }` to move it (default order 0, lower first).
Renderers (`tools`, `toolLines`, `entries`, `link`, `inlineCode`, `codeBlocks`, `messageActions`, `messageDetails`,
`answerLabels`, `userBubble`, `compact`, `inbox`, `composer`) are in [renderers](renderers.md), `documents` in
[documents](documents.md), `commands` in [commands](commands.md) and `provides` in [web points](contracts.md#web-points).

## Slots

Components mounted in named places of the shell, on every surface that renders the primitive holding them, and in the
title bar the host shows above every surface.

| Slot                   | Where                                                                                                        |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `sidebar`              | Left column (`<Sidebar />`); it disappears while nothing is in it                                            |
| `sidebar.top`          | Agent sidebar, after the Agents group and before the roots: background work such as watches                  |
| `titlebar.brand`       | Title bar, the wordmark beyond a phone; render `Wordmark` from `@/sdk` with an `onClick`                     |
| `titlebar.project`     | Title bar, in place of the project chip; render `ProjectChip` from `@/sdk` with a menu                       |
| `titlebar.left`        | Title bar above every surface, after the project chip; monospace, one line                                   |
| `titlebar.right`       | Title bar, right, before the palette button                                                                  |
| `header.right`         | Right side of the header, before the panel toggle (`<Header>`)                                               |
| `statusline.left`      | Bottom status line, left; monospace, one line (`<StatusLine />`)                                             |
