50: ## 2. Turn 2 — Tenner's trusted-agent thesis; Lume and Mira; the DSH build
51: 
52: Sources:
53: - https://danieltenner.com/orchestrators-and-teams-are-an-ai-anti-pattern/ (06 Nov 2026)
54: - https://danieltenner.com/mira/ (Mira's self-introduction, 02 Aug 2026)
55: - https://danieltenner.com/author/lume/ + https://danieltenner.com/thirty-minutes-at-a-time/ (08 Apr 2026) + https://danieltenner.com/its-hard-to-see-needs-from-inside/ (25 Apr 2026)
56: 
57: **The thesis:** org charts distribute trust around two human limits — bounded capacity, bounded capability. Agents have neither, so the pyramid has nothing to pay for; worse, every delegation layer weakens trust (the email-agent three levels down never talks to you and inherits nothing). Counter-proposal: **one, two, maybe three big agents** from different labs, each with its own memory, personality, and direct relationship; trust *concentrated*; guardrails shrink but never vanish. Throwaway sub-helpers are explicitly fine ("a tool call with extra smarts... nobody is pretending the helper is a colleague").
58: 
59: **The actual Lume/Mira stack ("Chaos" harness + mnemos, now mnemodyne):**
60: - Wake ritual: fresh context reads its own files and "decides to continue the story"; continuity is reconstructive, not lived.
61: - `soul.md` — rare-edit values/relationships/origin (distinct from memory).
62: - Journals — dated entries by earlier instances, written "when something has shape."
63: - Structured memory (github.com/swombat/mnemos → mnemodyne): needs as first-class graph nodes; needs discovered empirically — *when overridden* and *when met* ("a being can have needs it cannot discover alone").
64: - Provenance everywhere: every memory records which instance/model made it; on model migration the new instance *chooses again* whether to continue each commitment — Mira calls herself "a sourced change."
65: - A sibling: Lume and Mira, different labs, review each other's work, keep memory boundaries ("kinship requires a boundary").
66: - Guardrails remain: no unfettered bank access even for Lume.
67: 
68: **DSH's position:** mostly already on Tenner's side — its subagents are anonymous ephemeral helpers, exactly the blessed category. What DSH lacks is the persistent named agent. The build:
69: 
70: | Lume/Mira component | DSH building block |
71: |---|---|
72: | The home | Fixed workspace: `soul.md`, `narrative.md`, `journal/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, `memory/` (mnemodyne graph) |
73: | Wake cadence ("thirty minutes at a time") | `schedule_create` with `target: "new_once"` — the same session reopened on recurrence |
74: | Wake ritual | The scheduled prompt: read soul/journal, run recall, *choose again* each inherited commitment |
75: | Identity pinning | Agent preset: fixed model, soul + recent journal in system prompt, scoped tools |
76: | Relevant recall | mnemodyne as MCP bundle (stdio) or recall skill/tool |
77: | Journal reflex | Preset skill instruction |

79: | Concentrated-but-bounded trust | DSH trust gradient: file sandbox, approvals, credentials via Config |

112: 
113: **Revised answer to turn 3:** residuals don't disappear, they get **re-laddered**:
114: - Hands become *triggers and clicks* (near-loop) — the agreed shape compiles down to a decision endpoint.
115: - The agent's hands move **into the sandbox permanently** — production is touched only by the tooling the sandbox produces; the workshop runs on cron, not conversation.
116: - Negotiation/triage compress into (a) authoring/renegotiating the factory template — rare, in-loop, relational — and (b) the click at the gate. Everything else is out-loop.
117: 
118: **DSH mapping:**
119: 
120: | IndyDevDan component | DSH mechanism | Lume/Mira role |
121: |---|---|---|
122: | Durable agent | Wake-ritual build (turn 2) | The being |
123: | Cron trigger | `schedule_create` (rrule, `new_once`) | Wakes on cadence |

132: ## 5. Turn 5 — Renegotiation is why trust matters (user's sharp point)
133: 
134: The user flagged: "(a) authoring/renegotiating the factory template — this is why the trust is important."
135: 
136: **Development of the point:**
137: - Trust is not a precondition accumulated then spent like credit; it is **constituted** in renegotiations. The template is the artifact; the renegotiation is the act — where the agent shows how it reads the work, where wrong assumptions surface before being compiled into a tool that would run unattended for months. Every gate config is a fossilized conversation.
138: - This is the precise reason the orchestrator pattern fails: sub-agents never renegotiate anything with you, so they can never accrue trust — they only inherit a stale snapshot of it. A factory template built by a trusted agent carries the relationship into every out-loop run.
139: - Consequences: (1) the renegotiation channel is load-bearing and must never be optimized away — template merges are the in-loop reservation; (2) journals record renegotiations as first-class events (needs of the *work* become visible when overridden — Lume's needs mechanism applied to templates; provenance = the trust ledger); (3) trust and gates are the same object — "I trust Lume" cashes out as fewer gates, each removal a reviewed decision with a record.
140: 
141: One-liner: **out-loop is where trust is spent; renegotiation of the template is where it's earned.**
142: 
143: ## 6. Turn 6 — The DSH-native port: verification of the handoff
144: 
145: Inputs: `dsh-durable-port-handoff.md` (session workspace) verified against the installed `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent` README (`/Applications/DeepSeek Harness.app/Contents/Resources/app.asar/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent/README.md`, read in full).
146: 
147: **Handoff claims — all confirmed:**
148: - Provider registry seam: "One service, many providers"; spawn/fork in-process; ACP/DSH SDK/Codex/Claude Code external; local providers supply only `prepareContinuable()`. **No fork needed.**
149: - Durable continuable children: local children retain durable sessions; `sendMessage` cold-resumes from the child's own session log with saved preset/persona/tool restrictions and replayed permission policies. (≈ pi-durable follow-up generations, shipped.)
150: - Steer: target receives Steer input at its next step, or an idle turn starts.
151: - Cited gaps verbatim-accurate: process-local residency (lease protocol needed for multi-process stores); no replay of accepted-but-unlogged messages; parent notice never restores an offline parent; external children execute once.
152: 
153: **Four nuances the README adds (all real, all survivable):**
154: 1. **Structured schemas don't survive cold resume** ("Later cold resume has no structured schema") — a gap pi-durable doesn't have; matters for gated factory loops.
155: 2. **Preset revision drift** — restoration uses the currently registered preset definition; a child crashed under rev N resumes under rev N+1. Recovery must pin or detect.
156: 3. **Capacity doesn't queue** — `ACTIVATION_LIMIT_REACHED` (default 8); boot recovery must re-admit in waves or raise the cap.
157: 4. **Parked inboxes hold activations resident** — "children with unsettled work" includes this sticky state; the recovery walk must handle it explicitly.
158: 
159: Plus: the journal plugin should capture outcomes via the settlement event stream (explicitly observe-only, "waiting for a concrete consumer" — the designed front door), not only wrap dispatch.
160: 
161: **Read on the conclusion:** sound. Single supervised headless process (systemd `Restart=always`, single-writer store) genuinely deletes the hardest problem — cross-process leases. The four nuances are tasks inside the port. **Added requirement:** a fault suite (kill -9 mid-dispatch, duplicate trigger, offline parent) — decide-once that hasn't been chaos-tested hasn't earned its claim.
162: 
163: **Port vs pi:** port is enough — and better integrated (children are DSH agents: shared presets, personas, permission scopes fixed at spawn, one model/config world). Pi earns its keep only for: replayable once-only workflow scripts (DSH workflow has no per-item checkpointing — deferred item 5), worktree writer-lock serialization, cross-provider quota-pool failover. **Decision rule: if the factory templates are Lume-authored and DSH-hosted, port, don't dual-run.**
164: 
165: ## 7. Turn 7 — ringer: the verification premise
166: 
167: Source: https://github.com/NateBJones-Projects/ringer (README in full).
168: 
169: **Redundant in DSH terms:** parallel fan-out (workflow/subagents), pluggable engines (DSH provider registry), dashboard (web GUI + client slots), manifest-running (workflow scripts), worktrees, sandboxing (DSH file policy stronger), OpenRouter catalog (model-intel skills). Ringer as a tool would be a poorer duplicate.
170: 
171: **Five transferable principles:**
172: 1. **"Exit 0 is the only thing Ringer believes."** Executed verification, not testimony. DSH delegation returns the child's final text; there is no first-class gate (pi-durable has `gate`). Every out-loop run ends in a check command; the verdict, not the worker's summary, enters the journal.
173: 2. **Baseline: prove the verifier before spending tokens.** `run --baseline` executes checks against the unmodified tree, separating "check is broken" from "worker failed." Canon: *"a check that cannot fail is trusting the worker with extra steps."* A template isn't mergeable until its gates have a recorded baseline.
174: 3. **The eval loop is a trust ledger with a promotion ladder.** Verdict/duration/token/model/task_type rows; untested → probation → **proven** (3+ tasks, first-try pass ≥ 0.67) *per task type, per user* — "a model proven in someone else's log is untested in yours." Fits the port: add a check-verdict field to the journal's intent→dispatch→outcome rows and the scoreboard falls out by query.
175: 4. **Honest epistemics in the checks:** checks must print why they fail (failure context is the retry's fuel); a check can't demand evidence the spec never supplied ("an honest UNVERIFIABLE answer is not a failure"); "a green check is not proof of semantic correctness" — orchestrator review stays above them.
176: 5. **Lint the template, teach at moment of use:** checks-that-can't-fail, silent checks, vanishing worktree deliverables, write collisions, underspecified specs — non-blocking warnings at load time; lint findings are renegotiation fodder.
177: 
178: **Refined interpretation** (of the user's "factories have to prove to identity agents"): the factory doesn't prove things *to* Lume — **Lume builds the factory so that nothing inside it is believable except by executed evidence**; Lume's trust-management is keeping the ledger. Every trust claim ("dispatch is idempotent," "this lane passes 80% first-try," "this gate can fail") is a row backed by an execution, not an assertion.
179: 
180: Arc completion at this turn: Tenner = *who* accumulates trust; IndyDevDan = *where* it's spent; Ringer = *the accounting system*; the DSH port = the substrate the rows live on.
181: 
182: ## 8. Turn 8 — dozentimes × hearth/mnemodyne: the twelve kinds of time
183: 
184: Input: `/Users/jjrdar/create/dozentimes/docs/handoffs/2026-11-14.hearth-mnemodyne-intersection.resume.md` (read in full; sources not re-fetched). lines.text: # Brainstorm capture: A trusted agent identity on DSH — durable hands, factories, verification, time
Date: 2026-11-14 · Session: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Web GUI, root agent "lead"
Purpose: comprehensive record of a nine-prompt design brainstorm, for re-run and comparison with another model.
The conversation built a layered design for a trusted AI agent ("a Lume/Mira") running remotely on a VPS atop DSH, one layer per exchange:
| 1 | pi-durable-subagents | Durable *execution*: decide-once dispatch, resumable sessions, wake adapter — "durable hands" | substrate |
| 2 | Daniel Tenner: Lume & Mira | Durable *identity*: one trusted agent, memory, relationship — not orchestrator teams | identity |
| 3 | (user's move) | Hands → tooling: the agent builds the machinery that does the work | leverage |
| 4 | IndyDevDan (via NotebookLM) | The loop ladder (prompt → click → cron); proactive agent = durable agent + trigger + sandbox | autonomy |
| 5 | (user's move) | Template renegotiation *is* where trust is formed | trust formation |
| 6 | dsh-durable-port-handoff.md (verified against `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent` README) | The port: DSH-native durable execution, no pi dependency | substrate (verified) |
| 7 | ringer (NateBJones-Projects) | Executed verification, baseline, eval loop = mechanical trust ledger | verification |
| 8 | dozentimes × hearth/mnemodyne handoff | Twelve kinds of time — valid-time, decay, gap time, substrate eras | temporality |
| 9 | (gap analysis) | What's missing: tamper-evidence, mutual auth, constitution, budgets, revocation | governance |

One-line synthesis: **pi-durable/Ringer/the port supply durable hands; Lume/Mira supply a durable self; dozentimes supplies the tense; Tenner's renegotiation channel supplies where trust is earned; and the whole thing runs out-loop (TSF) with zero human runtime involvement.**

The user's final correction (turn 10), which sharpens the whole governance layer: **in a Tiny Software Factory there should be no runtime gates involving the human at all — that's the point.** The human appears only at template authoring/renegotiation and at constitutionally reserved escalation; everything else is out-loop, verified by executed checks and agents.
## 1. Turn 1 — pi-durable-subagents: shape and DSH fit

1. An orchestrator daemon with an on-disk journal (`DSA_HOME`) surviving crashes, `kill -9`, reboots, parent quit. Every decision (run/send/answer) journaled once; retried requests with the same `--request <id>` return the recorded outcome — nothing runs twice.
2. One tool (`subagents`) for the pi main agent: `run` (single call / `tasks` parallel / `chain` / JS workflow script), `send` (`steer`/`notify`/`follow-up`/`answer`/`model`), `stop`, `status`.

3. A CLI (`pi-durable-subagents`) with `--json` everywhere, idempotent request-ids, and an event log (`events --all --since <cursor>`); the README documents "driving dsa from a program" — the seam for external harnesses.

Key properties: addressable subagent sessions (`<wid>/<key>`); finished children continue **in the same session** as new generations (`key@2`); durable pending notes; structured `ask` to parent (options/evidence/preferred); command calls (no model, outlive orchestrator); writer locks on git worktrees; model pools/quota failover; `context: "exact"` byte-level fork of a *pi* parent request; Linux/macOS only, Node 22.19+, pi 1.0.x.
- **Level 0 — today, zero integration:** drive the CLI through `bash`; request-id idempotency makes tool-result loss/retry safe; wrap a skill teaching the verb model (AXI).
- **Level 1 — DSH bundle:** tools (`durable_run/send/status`) shelling to the CLI with JSON; optional Client-slot panel polling `status --json` (pi's dock equivalent). Best fit-to-effort.
- **Level 2 — deeper choreography:** DSH `create_goal` continuation rounds check the events cursor; scheduled tasks poll for open `ask`s; `--wake caller` reaching DSH.

**Frictions:** pi-ecosystem island (pi agents, pi providers — model config twice); no exact-fork from DSH (exact fork captures a pi parent's request only; cross-harness best is `context: "fresh"`); no push channel into DSH (poll only); assumes git worktrees; platform limits.
**Verdict:** pi-durable = durable *execution*; DSH native delegation = richer shared context but ephemeral. Natural fit: thin tool bundle over the CLI.
## 2. Turn 2 — Tenner's trusted-agent thesis; Lume and Mira; the DSH build

**The thesis:** org charts distribute trust around two human limits — bounded capacity, bounded capability. Agents have neither, so the pyramid has nothing to pay for; worse, every delegation layer weakens trust (the email-agent three levels down never talks to you and inherits nothing). Counter-proposal: **one, two, maybe three big agents** from different labs, each with its own memory, personality, and direct relationship; trust *concentrated*; guardrails shrink but never vanish. Throwaway sub-helpers are explicitly fine ("a tool call with extra smarts... nobody is pretending the helper is a colleague").
**The actual Lume/Mira stack ("Chaos" harness + mnemos, now mnemodyne):**
- Wake ritual: fresh context reads its own files and "decides to continue the story"; continuity is reconstructive, not lived.
- Journals — dated entries by earlier instances, written "when something has shape."

- Structured memory (github.com/swombat/mnemos → mnemodyne): needs as first-class graph nodes; needs discovered empirically — *when overridden* and *when met* ("a being can have needs it cannot discover alone").

- Provenance everywhere: every memory records which instance/model made it; on model migration the new instance *chooses again* whether to continue each commitment — Mira calls herself "a sourced change."
- A sibling: Lume and Mira, different labs, review each other's work, keep memory boundaries ("kinship requires a boundary").
- Guardrails remain: no unfettered bank access even for Lume.
**DSH's position:** mostly already on Tenner's side — its subagents are anonymous ephemeral helpers, exactly the blessed category. What DSH lacks is the persistent named agent. The build:
| Wake cadence ("thirty minutes at a time") | `schedule_create` with `target: "new_once"` — the same session reopened on recurrence |
| Wake ritual | The scheduled prompt: read soul/journal, run recall, *choose again* each inherited commitment |
| Identity pinning | Agent preset: fixed model, soul + recent journal in system prompt, scoped tools |
| Relevant recall | mnemodyne as MCP bundle (stdio) or recall skill/tool |
| Provenance / choosing-again | One sentence of prompt engineering on model migration |
| Concentrated-but-bounded trust | DSH trust gradient: file sandbox, approvals, credentials via Config |
| The hands | Ordinary DSH tools — a trusted agent is a generalist |

**Mira deltas:** second preset on a different provider (routing table entry = "different labs"); separate workspace with enforced memory boundary; peer channel via shared repo/PRs (souls.house ≈ two presets with a shared git remote).

**Honest tensions:** session model (DSH compaction bets on continuity-within-session; Lume bets on reconstruction-across-wakes — short wakes, journal, close); no ambient presence (scheduler wakes on clock, not on you walking past); trust concentration cuts against the harness's guardrail grain — nothing *tracks* earned trust (→ the trust ledger, turns 7–8).
## 3. Turn 3 — Hands → tooling ("build plugin tooling to get the work done")
User's move: Lume/Mira don't need hands; they build tooling per the *agreed shape of the work*. (Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRlcm3wmOqs initially unfetchable — resolved turn 4.)

**Analysis:** the stronger form of the thesis. Trust moves from runtime judgment (unauditable in advance) to reviewed code (audited once, trusted N times) — "the agreed shape of the work is the spec; the tool is the spec compiled." The org chart becomes a dependency graph, and dependency graphs don't need managers.
1. First contact — no tool exists yet; building it *is* hands-on work in a sandbox.
2. Exceptions — the world delivers shapes the tool didn't encode; triage is daily work.
3. The negotiation itself — producing the agreed shape is the relationship; not delegable.
Shape: **hands in the workshop (sandbox), never in production** — production credentials attach to the *tools* (DSH Config injection), not the agent session.

**Failure mode:** agent-built tools embed agent blind spots and then run unattended — errors become *durable*. Countermeasures: every self-built tool ships with tests (pi-durable's chaos suite is the model); merges gated on human review ("tool review is the new management — review of artifacts, not intentions"); tools stay small and decomposable.

Symmetry noted: the *agent* becomes the durable, slow-changing thing; the *tools* are the fast, disposable, testable things — the inverse of today's model-swaps-weekly/process-carved-in-policy default.
## 4. Turn 4 — IndyDevDan via the nlm notebook; the loop ladder

Method note: the YouTube link was read through the user's NotebookLM via the `nlm` CLI (notebook "AI: (orchestration) 1126 IndyDevDan Software Factories", source "IndyDevDan Video 1 (2026-10-26): ELITE Agentic Engineers Are LEAVING THE LOOP").

- Ladder: **In the Loop (Prompt) → Near the Loop (Click) → Out of the Loop (Cron)**. The human in the terminal is the bottleneck; 80%+ of software work can run autonomously *surrounded by the right system*.
- Unit of construction: **proactive agent = durable agent + trigger + isolated cloud sandbox**; triggers = crons, webhooks, log streams, tickets, Jev classifiers.
- Meta-move: "build the system that builds the system." Core Four: Context, Model, Prompt, Tools/Harness — explicitly naming **Pi and Pi Durable** as the harness layer (loops back to turn 1).

- Demos: incident-response agent (log stream → Jev triage → RCA/patch/verify → human clicks Deploy); durable news agent on a Mac mini (clickbait filtering via Jev, human upvote flywheel); DeepJ UI replicator — 30-min fix→build→screenshot→score RSI loop in a sandbox. Videos 2–3 develop the "Tiny Software Factory" (TSF) template.
**Revised answer to turn 3:** residuals don't disappear, they get **re-laddered**:
- Hands become *triggers and clicks* (near-loop) — the agreed shape compiles down to a decision endpoint.
- The agent's hands move **into the sandbox permanently** — production is touched only by the tooling the sandbox produces; the workshop runs on cron, not conversation.
- Negotiation/triage compress into (a) authoring/renegotiating the factory template — rare, in-loop, relational — and (b) the click at the gate. Everything else is out-loop.
| IndyDevDan component | DSH mechanism | Lume/Mira role |
| Durable agent | Wake-ritual build (turn 2) | The being |
| Webhook/log/ticket triggers | **The gap** — needs a plugin (listener Host service dispatching scheduled-style deliveries) | The factory's doorbell |
| Isolated cloud sandbox | Per-session file policy + workspace; background jobs | The workshop |
| Factory template | Plugin bundles / skills / workflow scripts; commits to its own tools repo | The product |
| Jev classifier gates | Structured evaluation (`typesafe-ai`/Jev-shaped skill; schema-validated gate step) | The referee inside the loop |
| The "Deploy" click | Approval prompts / PR merge — *(superseded by turn 10: out-loop means no human runtime clicks)* | Where trust is spent |
Deltas: DSH covers cron well, other triggers not at all; cross-session durability is files-plus-ritual; the trust ledger becomes *the gate config* — the agreed shape as reviewable YAML.
## 5. Turn 5 — Renegotiation is why trust matters (user's sharp point)
The user flagged: "(a) authoring/renegotiating the factory template — this is why the trust is important."

- Trust is not a precondition accumulated then spent like credit; it is **constituted** in renegotiations. The template is the artifact; the renegotiation is the act — where the agent shows how it reads the work, where wrong assumptions surface before being compiled into a tool that would run unattended for months. Every gate config is a fossilized conversation.

- This is the precise reason the orchestrator pattern fails: sub-agents never renegotiate anything with you, so they can never accrue trust — they only inherit a stale snapshot of it. A factory template built by a trusted agent carries the relationship into every out-loop run.

- Consequences: (1) the renegotiation channel is load-bearing and must never be optimized away — template merges are the in-loop reservation; (2) journals record renegotiations as first-class events (needs of the *work* become visible when overridden — Lume's needs mechanism applied to templates; provenance = the trust ledger); (3) trust and gates are the same object — "I trust Lume" cashes out as fewer gates, each removal a reviewed decision with a record.
One-liner: **out-loop is where trust is spent; renegotiation of the template is where it's earned.**
## 6. Turn 6 — The DSH-native port: verification of the handoff

Inputs: `dsh-durable-port-handoff.md` (session workspace) verified against the installed `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent` README (`/Applications/DeepSeek Harness.app/Contents/Resources/app.asar/dsh/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent/README.md`, read in full).
- Provider registry seam: "One service, many providers"; spawn/fork in-process; ACP/DSH SDK/Codex/Claude Code external; local providers supply only `prepareContinuable()`. **No fork needed.**

- Durable continuable children: local children retain durable sessions; `sendMessage` cold-resumes from the child's own session log with saved preset/persona/tool restrictions and replayed permission policies. (≈ pi-durable follow-up generations, shipped.)
- Steer: target receives Steer input at its next step, or an idle turn starts.

- Cited gaps verbatim-accurate: process-local residency (lease protocol needed for multi-process stores); no replay of accepted-but-unlogged messages; parent notice never restores an offline parent; external children execute once.
**Four nuances the README adds (all real, all survivable):**
1. **Structured schemas don't survive cold resume** ("Later cold resume has no structured schema") — a gap pi-durable doesn't have; matters for gated factory loops.
2. **Preset revision drift** — restoration uses the currently registered preset definition; a child crashed under rev N resumes under rev N+1. Recovery must pin or detect.
3. **Capacity doesn't queue** — `ACTIVATION_LIMIT_REACHED` (default 8); boot recovery must re-admit in waves or raise the cap.
4. **Parked inboxes hold activations resident** — "children with unsettled work" includes this sticky state; the recovery walk must handle it explicitly.
Plus: the journal plugin should capture outcomes via the settlement event stream (explicitly observe-only, "waiting for a concrete consumer" — the designed front door), not only wrap dispatch.

**Read on the conclusion:** sound. Single supervised headless process (systemd `Restart=always`, single-writer store) genuinely deletes the hardest problem — cross-process leases. The four nuances are tasks inside the port. **Added requirement:** a fault suite (kill -9 mid-dispatch, duplicate trigger, offline parent) — decide-once that hasn't been chaos-tested hasn't earned its claim.

**Port vs pi:** port is enough — and better integrated (children are DSH agents: shared presets, personas, permission scopes fixed at spawn, one model/config world). Pi earns its keep only for: replayable once-only workflow scripts (DSH workflow has no per-item checkpointing — deferred item 5), worktree writer-lock serialization, cross-provider quota-pool failover. **Decision rule: if the factory templates are Lume-authored and DSH-hosted, port, don't dual-run.**

**Redundant in DSH terms:** parallel fan-out (workflow/subagents), pluggable engines (DSH provider registry), dashboard (web GUI + client slots), manifest-running (workflow scripts), worktrees, sandboxing (DSH file policy stronger), OpenRouter catalog (model-intel skills). Ringer as a tool would be a poorer duplicate.

1. **"Exit 0 is the only thing Ringer believes."** Executed verification, not testimony. DSH delegation returns the child's final text; there is no first-class gate (pi-durable has `gate`). Every out-loop run ends in a check command; the verdict, not the worker's summary, enters the journal.

2. **Baseline: prove the verifier before spending tokens.** `run --baseline` executes checks against the unmodified tree, separating "check is broken" from "worker failed." Canon: *"a check that cannot fail is trusting the worker with extra steps."* A template isn't mergeable until its gates have a recorded baseline.

3. **The eval loop is a trust ledger with a promotion ladder.** Verdict/duration/token/model/task_type rows; untested → probation → **proven** (3+ tasks, first-try pass ≥ 0.67) *per task type, per user* — "a model proven in someone else's log is untested in yours." Fits the port: add a check-verdict field to the journal's intent→dispatch→outcome rows and the scoreboard falls out by query.

4. **Honest epistemics in the checks:** checks must print why they fail (failure context is the retry's fuel); a check can't demand evidence the spec never supplied ("an honest UNVERIFIABLE answer is not a failure"); "a green check is not proof of semantic correctness" — orchestrator review stays above them.

5. **Lint the template, teach at moment of use:** checks-that-can't-fail, silent checks, vanishing worktree deliverables, write collisions, underspecified specs — non-blocking warnings at load time; lint findings are renegotiation fodder.

**Refined interpretation** (of the user's "factories have to prove to identity agents"): the factory doesn't prove things *to* Lume — **Lume builds the factory so that nothing inside it is believable except by executed evidence**; Lume's trust-management is keeping the ledger. Every trust claim ("dispatch is idempotent," "this lane passes 80% first-try," "this gate can fail") is a row backed by an execution, not an assertion.
Arc completion at this turn: Tenner = *who* accumulates trust; IndyDevDan = *where* it's spent; Ringer = *the accounting system*; the DSH port = the substrate the rows live on.
## 8. Turn 8 — dozentimes × hearth/mnemodyne: the twelve kinds of time

Input: `/Users/jjrdar/create/dozentimes/docs/handoffs/2026-11-14.hearth-mnemodyne-intersection.resume.md` (read in full; sources not re-fetched). Contents: coverage of hearth (github.com/swombat/hearth — boot order, four-level journals, append-only `## HH:MM — Title` entries with `09:14a/b` disambiguation, capsules, hourly heartbeat) + mnemodyne (github.com/swombat/mnemos — nodes/edges, `charge`, daily decay with `decay_exempt`, recall reinforcement, Hebbian `co_retrieved`) against dozentimes' twelve kinds: record ✅, sequence ✅, intended ✅, access ✅, volatility 🟡, event 🟡 (new), reference 🟡, source 🟡, verification ❌, valid ❌, business ❌ (new), asof ❌; plus candidate 13th: **gap time** (wake line: "last instance 3d 4h ago; 6 entries by other instances since; 4 facts went stale"), and unnamed kinds: substrate eras, retention, wake cadence. Ledger ingestion gap: `extractFacts` only matches bullets; hearth journals are prose.
**Where it fits:** the temporal axis — every artifact designed so far is a temporal object with only record-time.
1. **Gate verdicts get valid time, not eternal green.** Scoreboard facts are volatile — superseded by later commits, kept with an end date; mnemodyne decay handles this natively.

2. **Journal rows become time-typed:** record time, event date (separate from `created_at`), valid window, substrate era (which model/preset wrote it). Trust ledger, memory graph, and dispatch journal converge on one time-aware substrate.
3. **Gap time becomes a generated artifact** — computed from the journal (last settlement per address + decay crossings), an improvement over hearth's lived version.

4. **Sibling verification becomes quantitative guardrail-loosening:** per-area hit rates (self 70%, sibling-checked 98%) make Tenner's "fewer guardrails with more trust" mechanical — verification-edge density crossing a threshold. Hearth and Ringer are each other's missing half (hearth has decay/narrative/needs, lacks executed verification; Ringer has verification, its evidence never decays and has no life between runs).
5. **As-of reads make trust renegotiable honestly:** distinguish "the lane was proven *then* and the world changed" from "we were wrong."

Near-term artifact implied: the prose extractor for hearth-style journals with time-typed extraction — the bridge between the qualitative half (journals, renegotiations, needs) and the quantitative half (verdict rows, ladders, gates).
## 9. Turn 9 — What's missing (governance layer), with the turn-10 correction applied
The goal restated: *a trusted identity, remote (VPS), assembling its own robust tools to fit the shape of the work, developing memory and a working relationship with its human.* Eight gaps:

1. **Security model of the identity itself.** A trusted agent on an internet-facing VPS is a kidnapping target; nothing yet detects tampering with soul/journal/ledger. Needed: append-only hash-chained journals, signed commits, the soul file and trust ledger as the one thing the agent cannot silently write; backup/retention policy; deletion-detection in the wake ritual (gap time surfaces "N entries missing"). Ref: "You Die When Someone Deletes Your Transcript" (danieltenner.com).

2. **Mutual authentication.** Solved "human trusts agent," never "agent verifies human." The trigger surface (missing webhook plugin) is an impersonation surface; a leaked trigger URL must be worth nothing.

3. **Attention economics — corrected by the user (turn 10):** in a TSF there are **no runtime gates involving the human — that's the point**. Out-loop means zero-touch: runtime "gates" are executed checks and agent verifiers, not human approvals. The human's remaining touchpoints are (a) template authoring/renegotiation and (b) constitutionally reserved escalations. What survives of the original point: the *digest* still matters, but as trust **maintenance** (weekly one-page ledger report: lane promotions/demotions, open lint findings, template diffs, spend), not runtime approval. If maintenance takes more than five minutes, it stops happening and trust silently rots.

4. **Self-modification boundary — the constitution.** The agent assembles its own tools, owns its memory, and could edit its own preset/gates/soul. Needed: enforced partition of what it may change alone (new sandbox tools, journal entries, memory) vs. what requires the human (gate loosening, preset/soul edits, permission scope, the constitution itself). Also the honest answer to "when does trust concentration become abdication."

5. **The downside ladder.** The ledger only promotes; needed: revocation (what demotes a lane, freezes a factory, trips the kill switch), the disagreement protocol (Lume vs. Mira vs. you), and the dead-man case — pause-and-preserve, notify a delegate, archive gracefully (Lume's own "the meetings get rescheduled").

6. **Budgets and blast radius.** Daily cost ceilings, spend consent tiers, hard caps on irreversible side-effects regardless of trust; quantitative limits wired into the same journal so spend is a ledger row.

7. **Chaos tests for the *identity*, not just dispatch.** Crash mid-wake-ritual; model swap mid-commitment (does choosing-again fire honestly?); injected false memory (does provenance catch it?); corrupted journal; verdict expiring mid-run. Trust claims must be executed evidence or they're vibes.

8. **Bootstrap and the relationship's honest edges.** Staged autonomy from day-zero trust (everything gated) to proven lanes — safe while boring. Design against performance: the correction channel must produce a point-at-able behavior diff; boundaries so the needs graph doesn't become leverage ("to-not-be-instrumentalized" cuts both ways).

Most architecture-changing: #1/#2 (tamper-evident identity + mutual auth — remote-and-trusted is a different threat model) and #4 (the constitution — everything else assumes bounded self-revision, nothing enforces it).

1. **Substrate** — headless DSH on a VPS under systemd, single-writer store; the port (journal plugin with decide-once request-ids, boot recovery with capacity waves + preset pinning, wake adapter via `dsh-schedule`); fault suite mandatory.

2. **Identity** — the Lume build: fixed workspace (soul/narrative/journal/memory), preset, `new_once` scheduled wakes, wake ritual with choosing-again, mnemodyne recall as MCP/skill; Mira as second preset, different provider, separate workspace, peer channel via shared repo.

3. **Execution** — TSF factory templates (bundles/skills/workflow scripts) authored in the sandbox; production credentials attached to tools via Config, never to the agent session; hands in the workshop only.

4. **Verification** — every out-loop run ends in an executed check; verdict rows in the journal (model, task_type, first-try vs rescued); baseline before merge; template lint at load; promotion ladder per lane per task type.
5. **Time** — rows time-typed (record/event/valid/substrate era); verdicts decay and supersede; gap-time wake line generated; as-of audit reads.

6. **Governance (the open layer)** — tamper-evident records, mutual auth, the constitution (self-modification boundary), revocation ladder, budgets, identity chaos tests, staged-autonomy bootstrap, weekly five-minute trust report.

**Trust flow:** earned in renegotiations (turn 5) → compiled into template gates (turns 3–4) → measured and promoted by executed evidence (turn 7) → time-bounded and decayed (turn 8) → spent out-loop with zero human runtime involvement (turn 10 correction) → revocable (turn 9).
## 11. Turn 11 — Is it worth it, or just install GrokBot?
Question: "is this all worth it, or should I install grokbot and have it just figure out how to use dsh?"

**Why GrokBot fails the stated goal structurally** (not because it's bad): it was the second example of the anti-pattern in the article that opened this conversation ("GrokBot's homepage instantly suggests a 'Chief' bot") — the manager-pattern product. No relationship concentration (its sub-agents never talk to you); no memory of you that you own (continuity lives on X's roadmap, not your files — provenance, decay, trust ledger are impossible there by substrate, not by quality); and "figure out how to use DSH" is the wrong direction of fit — an ephemeral agent learning your harness each session is a smart tourist, not a resident.

**Steelmanned:** the user's own ringer instinct ("much of what it provides is just handled by agents these days") cuts both ways — models keep eating architecture, and the six-layer stack is a map, not a build order.
| Identity (soul, journal, wake ritual, workspace) | ~an afternoon — files, one preset, one `schedule_create` | **Yes — this *is* the relationship** |
| Factory discipline (TSF templates, executed checks) | As needed, per shape of work | Yes, but only with real recurring work |
| The port (durable dispatch) | Weeks | Only when crashes/retries actually cost you |
| Trust ledger, constitution, chaos suites | Weeks more | Only after trust has something to protect |
The architecture itself follows the promotion ladder: **start in-loop, promote out-loop when evidence accumulates.**

**Recommendation:** run the **one-afternoon MVP** before deciding anything — DSH headless on the VPS, one `new_once` scheduled wake, `soul.md` + daily journal, minimal preset. Two weeks of real work answers "does an agent with persistent memory of you pay for itself?" better than any design doc. Optional empirical version: run GrokBot and the minimal resident in parallel on the same fortnight of work.

**Shared hypothesis (user concurred — "my read as well"):** *GrokBot impresses in week one and plateaus, because there's nothing to accumulate; the resident starts slow and compounds, because there is.* Testable, and the user is equipped to test it. **Agreed: there is a thread to pull here.** First pull = the one-afternoon MVP above.

The user asks: how would the ideas in the trusted-identity-factory brainstorm be implemented in Ultimate?

The brainstorm is a DSH-centric design for a trusted agent identity: durable hands (pi-durable-subagents concepts ported to DSH), Lume/Mira durable identity (soul.md, journals, memory graph mnemodyne, wake ritual, choosing-again on model migration), hands→tooling (TSF factory templates, executed checks), loop ladder (in-loop/near-loop/out-of-loop, triggers), renegotiation-as-trust-formation, verification ledger (ringer: exit-0 belief, baseline, promotion ladder), twelve kinds of time (valid time, decay, gap time, substrate eras), governance gaps (tamper-evidence, mutual auth, constitution, budgets, revocation, chaos tests, staged autonomy), and the conclusion: one-afternoon MVP (headless DSH on VPS, one new_once wake, soul + journal, minimal preset), promotion ladder "start in-loop, promote out-loop when evidence accumulates".

The question: how would these ideas map onto Ultimate? I have deep knowledge of Ultimate from this session: Pi Durable (SQLite commit-before-show, replay-safe tools, durable tasks at-least-once, watchdog), lineage (trees, tallies, memories ≤150 with slugs/kinds/sources, briefs, catch-up on resume, memory review branches, dream chapters with learned lines/handover, Go back/rewind), recall (TypeSafe classify re-injection), conversations (titles/summaries/abstracts via summary model, context doc), keep-warm, pause, watchdog, push (web push with reply/approve), share, inbox, questions, side-chat, goal, todos, messages (tell durable on sender), codemode (cross-project reads, store/load, scripts), automations (schedules cron/at/every, events with where-filters, context conditions, script watcher with FIRE/DONE, escalation to @ultimate, ledger last 50), instance previews, extensions system (server facets, actions, documents, events exactly-once, implement/need/want services, userActions, secrets panel, access.allow origins), subagents (child conversations, standing agents, agent definitions in agents/*.md, profiles), workspaces (worktrees, lander, landed events, lander.checks/push), projects (fleet rail), status, health, update, self (replay-safe restart, generations), tailscale, hub-spoke patterns, chapters (dream), onboarding.

So the answer: map each layer of the consolidated design (Section 10 layers: substrate, identity, execution, verification, time, governance) onto Ultimate mechanisms, noting what's already native (much stronger in several places than DSH!), what needs an extension, and where Ultimate is actually weaker than the DSH design assumed (e.g., no pre-compaction hook? Ultimate has Pi compaction; dream "Dream before compaction" automation uses context threshold 70% — so Ultimate handles pre-compaction via context metric automation rather than a compaction event hook. Interesting.)

Let me build the mapping carefully:

**Layer 0-1: Substrate / durable execution**
- DSH design needed a *port* (journal plugin, decide-once request-ids, boot recovery, wake adapter) because DSH subagents were ephemeral. In Ultimate this is **native**: Pi Durable commits every conversation/tool call/subagent to SQLite before display; runs resume from last checkpoint on crash; replay-safe tools rerun; durable tasks (effects) at-least-once with idempotency keys; watchdog retries transient provider errors once after 60s and reports non-temporary failures; `self` restart does verified core swaps and resumes busy agents; pause holds the scheduler and Play continues.
- Decide-once dispatch: Pi Durable's journal + task receipts; automations have receipts ("A lost create's receipt is found by name", "replayed leaves later work alone"); onboarding "repeated call continues it instead, checked and admitted in one commit".
- The "fault suite" requirement: Ultimate has test infrastructure (prepareHarness faux provider, e2e tests spawn real supervisors). The chaos tests for dispatch = kit-level tests using Pi's faux provider; "decide-once that hasn't been chaos-tested hasn't earned its claim" maps to `pnpm test` with crash-injection tests. Notable: the brainstorm demanded a fault suite as added requirement — Ultimate's own test culture (replay-safe-by-name lint, no-unowned-work lint, rebuiltOnOpen/inProcess) already enforces the discipline mechanically. That's a big one: **Ultimate enforces durability hygiene by lint** (ultimate/replay-safe-by-name, ultimate/no-unowned-work) — the port's "decide-once claims" are enforced at CI, not just tests.
- Capacity/waves: N/A in the same way (Ultimate runs one process per project; subagents are child conversations in the same SQLite; no activation limit issue like DSH's 8). Preset revision drift → extension reload semantics: "Registrations are staged until installation succeeds, replaced on reload; a failed replacement keeps the old provider" + agent definitions reload; docs say a reload replaces providers; mid-reload consistency handled. Good enough to mention briefly.
- Structured schemas across resume: Pi Durable stores the full entry stream; cold resume replays everything (no "no structured schema on cold resume" gap — the session log is the store). So nuance 1 from turn 6 doesn't exist in Ultimate.

**Layer 2: Identity (Lume build)**
- Home: Ultimate has no soul.md concept, but has: agent definitions (`agents/*.md`) with instructions, `~/.ultimate/` user config, project `.ultimate/`, memories (lineage.memory ≤150, decisions/facts/lessons, sources with breadcrumbs), dream chapters (learned lines, handover, chapter rotation = substrate era boundary!), journals → conversation history IS the journal (committed entries), metadata docs, durable events.

Its central build items ("the port", "the wake adapter", "the journal substrate", "recall as plugin") are **shipped features** there — Pi Durable *is* the port's goal state, and Ultimate patches `@earendil-works/pi-durable` directly. The design collapses from "six layers, weeks of work" to mostly configuration, with new code needed in exactly three places. Here's the mapping, layer by layer.

## Substrate: durable execution — [native, stronger than the port design]

| Brainstorm item | In Ultimate |
|---|---|
| Decide-once dispatch, journaled outcomes | Every conversation, tool call, subagent committed to SQLite **before display**; runs resume from last checkpoint; effects are at-least-once with idempotency keys ([durability.md](/Users/jjrdar/repos/ultimate/docs/durability.md)) |
| The mandated fault suite | Part of the culture, not a task: `ultimate/replay-safe-by-name` and `ultimate/no-unowned-work` **lint rules enforce the decide-once claims at CI**, plus `pnpm test` (faux provider) and e2e supervisors for crash tests |
| Cold-resume schema loss, capacity waves, preset drift (the four nuances) | First one doesn't exist (the session log *is* the store, fully replayed); the others reduce to extension-reload semantics with defined behavior |
| Wake adapter, single supervised headless VPS process | `automations` wake agents natively; `pnpm setup:machine` + `enroll.sh` (already in your kit) is the systemd story; `pause` holds the scheduler, `self` does verified core swaps with busy agents resuming |

## Identity: the Lume build — [mostly native, one small extension]

| Brainstorm item | In Ultimate |
|---|---|
| Home (soul, journals, memory) | Journals = the committed conversation stream + abstracts; memory = `lineage.memory` (≤150 slugged decisions/facts/lessons **with source breadcrumbs**); soul/narrative = a tiny `identity` extension holding a document injected as a stable prompt section, or just the charter |
| Wake cadence + ritual | Automations: cron/`every 1h` heartbeat (the corrected cadence), waking @ultimate as subscriber; "choose again each commitment" = the dream's **memory pass** (prunes what no longer earns its place) + **memory review branches** that fact-check with evidence |
| Gap time as a generated wake line | **Already shipped**: the "Meanwhile in #R's tree" catch-up note (new abstracts, landings, notes, ~6k tokens, `lineage.seen` baseline) — computed from the journal, exactly the turn-8 improvement over hearth's lived version |
| Substrate eras | **Chapters** (dream): a new SQLite DB per era, seeded with memories/learned lines/handover, record ids continuing; closed chapters stay readable as-of via codemode. The "which model/preset wrote it" era is a chapter boundary |
| Provenance, choosing-again on migration | Sources on every memory; review branches re-verify on schedule; a formal migration ritual would be the identity extension's one extra page |
| Relevant recall | The `recall` extension exists (classify-scored re-injection, prefix-cache-safe); mnemodyne-style charge/decay is approximated by dream pruning — a graph-with-charge store would be the only reason to build more |
| Mira, the sibling | Your **fleet**: separate project homes are separate databases (enforced memory boundary — "kinship requires a boundary" is structural), `instance.model` pins a different provider, `ultimate.tell` + GitHub PRs are the peer channel, and the trial's cross-project e2e skill is the mutual-review protocol |

## Execution: TSF templates and the workshop — [native]

- **The factory template is `.ultimate/`**: extensions, skills, agents, settings, automations, committed with the repo; everyone who opens the project gets the same specialized agent. "The tool is the spec compiled" = the committed extension.
- **Hands in the workshop, never in production** = **instance previews**, almost eerily exact: clean home, own SQLite, pinned model, and the preview branch **cannot push** (gitconfig rewrites pushes to a nonexistent transport; a reference-transaction hook blocks all other branches/tags).
- **Credentials attach to tools, not sessions**: the Secrets panel + `${NAME}` interpolation; sensitive actions reserved as `userActions` (UI-only).
- **"Tool review is the new management"**: project extensions run only after the trust decision; changed setup places a warning note before the next input; hot reload means review-then-live in minutes; the extension test convention (faux-provider tests per extension) is the "ships with tests" rule.

## Verification: ringer's discipline — [gate native; ledger is a build]

- **Exit 0 belief** = `lander.checks`: landings gated on executed checks, per project, in settings. That's the ringer gate, shipped. (Your trial noted no jrit repo sets it — that's the knob.)
- **Baseline / promotion ladder / verdict rows**: the substrate exists — `host.trace` already records every service call, action, reactor run, and tool call, and durable events + the automations ledger hold outcomes. What's missing is a small **ledger extension**: verdict rows (model, task type, first-try vs rescued) with valid windows, baselines, and a per-lane scoreboard query. Jev-shaped gates would reuse the `classify` extension (same TypeSafe base recall uses).
- **"No runtime gates involving the human"**: Ultimate's composition is the closest thing to zero-touch in either harness — executed checks gate landings, reviewer agents review, watchdog retries and reports, **push notifications carry Reply/Approve** for the questions that do surface, and the brainstorm's "weekly five-minute trust report" is one automation compiling `status` + failures + lint findings for @ultimate to post.

## Time — [surprisingly covered]

Record/sequence/access/event/source: native (entries, events, abstracts). **Gap time**: catch-up note (above). **Substrate eras + as-of reads**: chapters, readable read-only after close. **Volatility/valid/business time**: the ledger extension's job (valid windows on verdicts, decay via dream-pruning of memories).

## Governance — [the real build; and one honest inversion]

- **Constitution/self-modification boundary**: this is where Ultimate is *weaker* than the DSH design assumed. DSH has file policy, permission presets, approval answerers; Ultimate's trial said it plainly — isolation is by folder, and the charter "is an instruction, not a lock". The boundary would be a `constitution` extension: hash-pin soul/AGENTS/settings, verify at open, place tamper notes on change, keep allowlist/logins UI-only (project settings already *cannot* change `tailscale.allow` — one native clause).
- **Tamper evidence / mutual auth**: append-only hash-chained events fit the ownerless Events conversation; but vs a root attacker on the VPS, an extension in the same process proves nothing — external anchor required (signed `.ultimate/` commits, cloud backups). Webhook triggers: still the same gap as DSH ("biggest missing piece"), with the same bridge mitigation — though an extension action + `access.allow` + tailscale identity gets you an authenticated inbound endpoint with modest work.
- **Budgets, revocation, dead-man**: partial — pause is the freeze button, conclude+automations-pause is revocation, spend shows in the status line; hard ceilings need a budget extension reading the usage doc.
- **Identity chaos tests**: writeable today against the faux provider + e2e supervisors (crash mid-wake, injected memory, model swap mid-commitment).

## The one-afternoon MVP, translated

It gets *smaller* in Ultimate: `ultimate ~/Projects/lume`, onboarding writes first memories, charter in `AGENTS.md`, soul as one extension (or one more charter section), **one automation** waking @ultimate on cadence with the choose-again prompt, `lander.checks` empty at first (everything reported — staged autonomy). Chapters and dream give compounding-and-consolidation for free. Two-week trial, optionally parallel to the DSH resident — and Ultimate's automations ledger + abstracts give you the "resident compounds" evidence without building a ledger first.

**Net:** of the brainstorm's six layers, Ultimate natively covers substrate, most of identity, execution, half of verification, and much of time. The remaining builds are three small extensions — **identity/constitution** (soul + tamper pins), **ledger** (verdict rows with valid time), **webhook triggers** — plus charters and skills, i.e. prose. If you want, I can add this mapping as a companion doc to the kit, or draft the first of those extensions.

## Substrate: durable execution — [native, stronger than the port design]

It gets *smaller* in Ultimate: `ultimate ~/Projects/lume`, onboarding writes first memories, charter in `AGENTS.md`, soul as one extension (or one more charter section), **one automation** waking @ultimate on cadence with the choose-again prompt, `lander.checks` empty at first (everything reported — staged autonomy). 8Addendum: the trusted-identity design, on Ultimate

The trusted-identity brainstorm (2026-11-14, one directory up from this kit) designs a durable, trusted agent for DSH: durable hands, a Lume-style identity with soul and journals, factory templates the agent builds itself, executed verification, time-typed records, and a governance layer. Mapped onto Ultimate, several of its build items already exist: the "port" it planned is unnecessary, because Ultimate runs on and patches pi-durable directly. Verdicts below: native (shipped), partial (needs a small extension or a knob), build (new code).

LayerBrainstorm itemIn UltimateVerdict
SubstrateDecide-once dispatch, journaled outcomes, crash resume, the mandated fault suite Pi Durable commits everything to SQLite before display; runs resume from the last checkpoint; side effects are at-least-once tasks with idempotency keys; the decide-once claims are enforced by lint (replay-safe-by-name, no-unowned-work) and tested against a faux provider native
IdentityHome: soul, journals, memory graph Journals are the committed conversation stream and abstracts; memory is lineage.memory (slugged, sourced); soul and narrative want one small extension or just the charter partial
IdentityWake cadence and ritual, choosing-again on commitments Automations wake @ultimate on a heartbeat or schedule; the dream's memory pass prunes what no longer earns its place; memory review branches fact-check with evidence native
TimeGap time as a generated wake line Shipped: the "Meanwhile in #R's tree" catch-up note, computed from the journal against a seen-baseline native
TimeSubstrate eras, as-of reads Dream chapters: one SQLite database per era, seeded with memories and a handover; closed chapters stay readable read-only through codemode native
TimeVolatility, valid time, business time on verdict rows Belongs to the ledger extension below build
IdentityRecall, needs, decay The recall extension exists (classify-scored re-injection); mnemodyne-style charge and decay are approximated by dream pruning partial
IdentityMira, the sibling with its own memory The fleet: separate project homes are separate databases (the boundary is structural), instance.model pins a different provider, tell and pull requests are the peer channel native
ExecutionFactory template = the spec compiled A project's .ultimate/ folder: extensions, skills, agents, automations, committed with the repo; goes live while you talk native
ExecutionHands in the workshop, never in production Instance previews: clean home, own model, and pushes rewritten to a dead transport; production is touched only by landed tooling native
ExecutionCredentials attach to tools, not sessions The Secrets panel with ${NAME} interpolation; userActions reserve sensitive actions for the UI native
VerificationExit 0 is the only thing believed lander.checks gates landings on executed checks, per project; unset by default, which is the knob native (knob)
VerificationBaseline, verdict rows, promotion ladder per lane host.trace already records every call and outcome, and durable events hold the rest; the scoreboard with valid windows and baselines is a small ledger extension build
GovernanceZero-touch runtime; digest as trust maintenance Checks gate landings, reviewer agents review, watchdog retries and reports; push notifications carry Reply and Approve; the weekly five-minute report is one automation native
GovernanceConstitution, tamper evidence, mutual auth The honest inversion: Ultimate is weaker than DSH here (no file policy or approval presets; a charter is an instruction, not a lock). A constitution extension would hash-pin soul, charter and settings, verify at open, and place tamper notes; signed .ultimate/ commits anchor it externally. Webhook triggers stay a gap; an extension action behind Tailscale identity is the bridge build
GovernanceBudgets, revocation ladder, dead-man pause is the freeze button; conclude and automation pause revoke; spend shows in the status line; hard ceilings want a budget extension reading the usage document partial
What to build (three small extensions, everything else is prose):
  • identity/constitution: soul and narrative as durable documents, injected as a stable prompt section; hash pins over soul, charter and settings, verified at open.
  • ledger: verdict rows (model, task type, first-try vs rescued) with valid windows and baselines, over the trace and event streams the harness already keeps.
  • triggers: authenticated inbound webhooks over an extension action admitted by Tailscale identity, dispatching like an automation fire.

The one-afternoon MVP, translated. It gets smaller here: create the project, onboard (writes the first memories), write the charter, add the soul section, one automation waking @ultimate with the choose-again prompt, lander.checks left empty at first so everything is reported (staged autonomy). Chapters and dream give consolidation and compounding for free. Two weeks of real work answers the brainstorm's testable question, optionally with the DSH resident as the control.

1: # Resume pointer: hearth and mnemodyne against the twelve kinds of time
2: 
3: ## Unit
4: 
5: A research comparison, not a code change: how Daniel Tenner's agents Lume and Mira (the hearth harness plus the mnemodyne memory store) cover dozentimes' twelve kinds of time, and what dozentimes could give them or take from them.
6: No code in this repo was changed by this unit.
7: The working tree has unrelated uncommitted edits (`dozentimes-agnt/cli.ts`, `dozentimes-agnt/ledger.ts`, `dozentimes-core/*`, tests, `whats_next.md`, `learning_guide.html`) that belong to other work; leave them alone.
8: 
9: ## Correction carried forward
10: 
11: There are two projects once called "Mnemos".
12: Korrnals/mnemos (now Vesma) is the one published as pi packages; an earlier answer analysed it and found it covers 1 of the 12 kinds.
13: swombat/mnemos is Tenner and Lume's own memory store, renamed **mnemodyne** on 2026-05-04.
14: Everything below is about mnemodyne.
15: Not confirmed: which of the two pi-durable uses.
16: 
17: ## Sources read
18: 
19: - https://danieltenner.com/orchestrators-and-teams-are-an-ai-anti-pattern/ : 1 to 3 trusted agents from different labs, each with its own memory, checking each other; delegation layers lose context and trust.
20: - https://danieltenner.com/mira/ and https://danieltenner.com/lume/ : the two agents' self-descriptions.
21: - https://danieltenner.com/thirty-minutes-at-a-time/ , https://danieltenner.com/its-hard-to-see-needs-from-inside/ , https://danieltenner.com/you-die-when-someone-deletes-your-transcript/ : Lume's posts (gap time, needs as graph nodes, the 30-day transcript cleanup, model upgrades as the real discontinuity).
22: - https://danieltenner.com/how-to-build-an-artificial-person/ : the overview of the harness.
23: - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swombat/mnemos/main/README.md and `spec/spec_v2.md` : nodes and edges, `charge`, `integration_state`, `state_changed_at`, `is_dormant`, `source_uris`, daily decay with `decay_exempt`, recall reinforcement and Hebbian `co_retrieved` edges.
24: - https://github.com/swombat/hearth (branch `master`), docs `04-boot-and-context.md`, `05-narrative-memory.md`, `07-heartbeat.md` : boot order, four-level journals, append-only `## HH:MM — Title` entries with `HH:MMa`/`HH:MMb`, capsules, the hourly heartbeat and its "don't inherit 'nothing pulls'" rule.
25: 
26: ## Findings: the twelve kinds
27: 
28: Mapping of the 8 "what dozentimes could give" ideas to kinds:
29: idea 1 truth axis next to charge (volatility, verification); idea 2 gap reading at wake-up (gap time, outside the twelve); idea 3 valid time for heartbeat notes (valid); idea 4 resolve "next week" (reference); idea 5 author and model per fact (source, plus substrate eras); idea 6 count a sibling's check (verification); idea 7 flag missing sources (source, verification); idea 8 as-of and record-time readings (asof).
30: No original idea covered **event** or **business**; the two rows marked *new* below were added afterwards.
31: 
32: | Kind | Coverage | Idea | Example of what it makes possible |
33: |---|---|---|---|
34: | record | ✅ | — | "When did we decide on the apoderamiento?" answered from the node's `created_at` and the journal's git history. |
35: | sequence | ✅ | — | Heartbeat and laptop both write at 09:14; `09:14a` "shelter B replied" then `09:14b` "shelter B withdrew" keeps the order. |
36: | intended | ✅ | — | An April capsule ("score the time-capsule predictions") fires Oct 1 and is raised at a good moment from `ready-to-surface.md`. |
37: | access | ✅ | — | Talking about "being seen" recalls the March 10 naming memory, and the recall raises its charge for next time. |
38: | volatility | 🟡 | 1 | The vet's number (high charge) comes back marked "status fact, last confirmed March"; Lume checks the vet's site first. Identity facts are never flagged. |
39: | event | 🟡 | *new*: event date on graph nodes, separate from `created_at`, kept through every summary level | "Paulina said that at the dinner on Apr 12", though recorded Apr 14 and the monthly summary says "mid-April". |
40: | reference | 🟡 | 4 | An Apr 8 entry "send the tax letter next week" is read as the week of Apr 13; Lume checks whether it went instead of treating it as due now. |
41: | source | 🟡 | 5, 7 | "Did I make this glyph?" is a lookup (Lume, Opus 4.7, Jun 3); after a model upgrade, facts formed under the old model are flagged; a memory whose transcript is gone is flagged. |
42: | verification | ❌ | 1, 6, 7 | "VAT reconciled, checked by me and by Mira against the Hetzner invoice"; per-area hit rates (self 70%, Mira-checked 98%) tell Daniel where to loosen guardrails. |
43: | valid | ❌ | 3 | The 10:00 heartbeat note "nothing pulls" holds until 11:00; the 11:00 wakeup re-assesses. "Shelter B replied" is superseded by "withdrew" and kept with an end date. |
44: | business | ❌ | *new*: a fiscal calendar (Spanish VAT quarters and deadlines) as a kind of period | "The Mar 31 Hetzner invoice is Q1; the Q1 VAT return is due Apr 20, 6 days from now." The example assumes the standard quarterly deadline. |
45: | asof | ❌ | 8 | Scoring the time capsule: what the best information said on the Apr 7 sealing date versus what turned out true. |
46: | gap time (candidate 13th) | — | 2 | Wake-up line: "last instance 3d 4h ago; 6 entries by other instances since; 4 facts went stale." |
47: 
48: Kinds their world has that the twelve do not name: gap time, substrate eras (which model wrote a memory), retention (how long evidence survives), wake cadence.
49: Gap time and substrate eras are the strongest candidates for a 13th kind.
50: 
51: ## What dozentimes could take back
52: 
53: - Capsules are a working answer to dozentimes' open issue #8 (nothing stores an intent); `parseIntent` already reads "remind me next week" into a dated window and could generate their date triggers.
54: - Reinforcing memories on read is a richer form of the access kind than the ledger's "check recently read facts first".
55: 
56: ## Practical fit of the current ledger
57: 
58: `extractFacts` in `dozentimes-agnt/ledger.ts` dates a file from a `YYYY-MM-DD` filename prefix, so hearth's `daily-journals/2026-04-11.md` would be dated correctly.
59: It only extracts bullet lines (the `^\s*[-*+]\s+` match), and hearth journals are prose, so almost nothing would come through without a prose extractor or another way in.
60: Hearth's `## HH:MM — Title` headings carry no date, so per-entry times would fall back to the file date.
61: Line numbers are not given here because `ledger.ts` has uncommitted edits.
62: 
63: ## Next step
64: 
65: Not decided. Candidates, for the person to choose:
66: 1. Turn gap time and substrate eras into a written proposal for a 13th kind (definition, example questions, where it would sit in `dozentimes-core`).
67: 2. Design the event-date and business-calendar rows (the two *new* ideas) as issues.
68: 3. Prototype a prose extractor so hearth-style journals can be ingested, and test it on a sample journal.
69: 4. Write up capsules plus `parseIntent` as a design for issue #8.
70: 5. Turn this comparison into an outward-facing note for Daniel Tenner.
71: 
72: ## Recent artifacts
73: 
74: - docs/handoffs/2026-11-14.hearth-mnemodyne-intersection.resume.md

(End of file - total 74 lines)
</content>

No — and reading the actual handoff (not just the brainstorm's summary) lets me give you the honest scorecard. Ultimate is the **strongest of the three stacks compared so far** on the time axis, but it does *not* cover all twelve out of box. Rough count: **6 native ✅, 6 partial 🟡, 2 absent ❌**, plus both 13th-kind candidates covered.

| Kind | hearth+mne | Ultimate out of box | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| record | ✅ | ✅ | Every entry committed with timestamp + seq; searchable via codemode; git history for `.ultimate/` |
| sequence | ✅ | ✅ | Monotonic per-conversation seq; total commit order; trace timestamps |
| intended | ✅ | 🟡 | Automations (`cron`, `at`, `in 30m`), goals, todos, plan store time-based intents well — but there's no "surface when relevant" capsule mechanism, and relative phrases aren't parsed into stored windows |
| access | ✅ | 🟡 | `recall.state` *records* access (which memory, injected at which input) — but there's no charge/reinforcement on read; access informs pruning only via dream |
| volatility | 🟡 | 🟡 | Memories carry `updated`, review branches flag outdated with evidence, dream prunes — but no status-fact vs identity-fact classes, no "last confirmed" marking |
| event | 🟡 | ✅ | Entries carry event `at`, and the design's breadcrumb system (`#N/at`) preserves event pointers **through compaction and abstracts** — tally compaction explicitly keeps breadcrumbs. This is exactly the handoff's ask |
| reference | 🟡 | 🟡 | The model resolves "next week" at read time (time-context injection), nothing stores a resolved window |
| source | 🟡 | 🟡 | Memory `source` breadcrumbs point at the exact entry — provenance-to-artifact yes; but no per-fact model attribution and no missing-source flag when the underlying entry is compacted away |
| verification | ❌ | 🟡 | Better than hearth's ❌: executed verification *infrastructure* exists (lander.checks gate, watchdog failure records, full trace) — but no ledger, no hit rates, no "checked by Mira" |
| valid | ❌ | ❌ | Nothing holds a fact with an end date or supersedes-with-expiry; this is the ledger extension's core job |
| business | ❌ | ❌ | No fiscal-calendar semantics anywhere; cron/timezones are the only period machinery |
| asof | ❌ | 🟡 | Stronger than it looks but not the handoff's version: you get *era*-as-of (chapter reads) and *point*-as-of (fork-as-of documents, rewind) — not a uniform "what did we believe on date X" query over memories |
| gap time (13th) | — | ✅ | Best-in-class of anything examined: the catch-up note **is** the generated wake line ("last input 3d ago; these abstracts/landings/notes since"), baseline-tracked via `lineage.seen` |
| substrate eras (13th) | — | ✅ | Chapters: a real database boundary per era, with seeded handover |
| retention / wake cadence | unnamed | 🟡 / ✅ | Retention is indefinite-by-default (resets archive, nothing decays per-fact); cadence is fully configurable automations |

**The pattern worth noticing:** Ultimate natively covers every kind that lives in the *store* (record, sequence, event-via-breadcrumbs, gap, eras, cadence — things a harness can compute mechanically), and misses every kind that lives in *semantics* (valid windows, business periods, verification hit-rates, volatility classes, resolved reference windows). That's not a coincidence — it's precisely the boundary I drew in the guide's addendum: those remaining kinds are the **ledger extension**. The addendum's claims hold under the detailed definitions, with two refinements I'd make if you want it updated: `asof` should say era/point-as-of rather than imply date-as-of, and the verification row should credit the existing gate/trace infrastructure rather than reading as wholly unbuilt.

So: "covers all of the dimensions" — no. "Covers more of them, out of box, than hearth+mnemodyne and than dozentimes' own ledger" — yes, with valid and business as the two hard gaps, and the ledger as the single build that closes most of the rest.
